**Part b) Winemaking comparison across four wines (20 marks)**

All four wines share the fundamental Madeira production framework: Vitis vinifera grapes harvested from the island's steep terraces; fermentation stopped by fortification (grape spirit addition at different stages of fermentation to achieve the appropriate RS level per variety); estufagem (heating process, either in tanks — canteiro system or industrial estufa) or canteiro maturation (ageing in old barrels in warm loft spaces — the premium method used by these producers for 10+ year wines); oxidative maturation in used barrique or old casks; and eventual bottling under NV designation after meeting minimum age statement criteria.

Key differences by style:
- *Sercial (dry):* fermentation continues to near-dryness before fortification; highest acid of the four; aged for minimum 10 years in the canteiro (barrel in warm loft) system; pale amber gold; driest finish (often <10 g/l RS effectively).
- *Verdelho (medium-dry):* fermentation stopped slightly earlier than Sercial; slightly more RS (~20-40 g/l); broader and nuttier than Sercial but still marked by Madeira's characteristic high acid.
- *Bual (medium-sweet):* fermentation stopped with moderate sweetness (~60-90 g/l RS); deeper amber color; richer, with more dried fig and caramel notes; still very high acid.
- *Malmsey (sweet):* fermentation stopped earliest — highest RS (~90-150 g/l); deepest color; most opulent, most sweet, most accessible to non-specialist consumers; the Madeira "gateway" variety.

The canteiro system (used for premium 10- and 15-year age statements) ages the wines in warm loft spaces where natural summer heat drives the estufagem, producing a more complex, less aggressive result than industrial estufa tanks.

*Wine 12 (Inniskillin Riesling Icewine):* Mechanism — **Cryoextraction (natural)**: grapes harvested frozen at -8°C or below; the ice crystals of water are left behind during pressing, concentrating juice sugars, acids, and aromas. **Part b) Winemaking comparison across four wines (20 marks)**

All four wines share the fundamental Madeira production framework: Vitis vinifera grapes harvested from the island's steep terraces; fermentation stopped by fortification (grape spirit addition at different stages of fermentation to achieve the appropriate RS level per variety); estufagem (heating process, either in tanks — canteiro system or industrial estufa) or canteiro maturation (ageing in old barrels in warm loft spaces — the premium method used by these producers for 10+ year wines); oxidative maturation in used barrique or old casks; and eventual bottling under NV designation after meeting minimum age statement criteria.

- *Bual (medium-sweet):* fermentation stopped with moderate sweetness (~60-90 g/l RS); deeper amber color; richer, with more dried fig and caramel notes; still very high acid.
- *Malmsey (sweet):* fermentation stopped earliest — highest RS (~90-150 g/l); deepest color; most opulent, most sweet, most accessible to non-specialist consumers; the Madeira "gateway" variety.

The canteiro system (used for premium 10- and 15-year age statements) ages the wines in warm loft spaces where natural summer heat drives the estufagem, producing a more complex, less aggressive result than industrial estufa tanks.

**Part a) Residual sugar — per wine**

*Wine 8 (Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, 2023):* Approximately 100-120 g/l RS. Fortified VDN (Vin Doux Naturel), Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. ABV 15%.

*Wine 12 (Inniskillin Riesling Icewine, 2022, Niagara):* Approximately 180-220 g/l RS. ABV ~9%.

**Part b) Alcohol levels — per wine**

As stated on the wine labels: Wine 8 = 15%; Wine 9 = 17.5%; Wine 10 = 7%; Wine 11 = 10.5%; Wine 12 = 9%.

**Part c) Origin and variety — per wine**

*Wine 8:* Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise (VDN), Rhône Valley, France. Grape: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. Bright aromatic orange blossom, lychee, fresh grape, medium gold color, sweet and fragrant but not as concentrated as Australian Muscat.

*Wine 9:* Rutherglen, Victoria, Australia. Grape: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains (Rutherglen Muscat). Deep amber-brown, extraordinarily concentrated raisin/coffee/Christmas cake/treacle aromas, extraordinary viscosity. Rutherglen Muscat is produced by the solera-like fractional blending system over decades.

*Wine 10:* Mosel, Germany. Grape: Riesling. Extremely high acid even with the enormous sweetness, peach/apricot/honey/noble rot botrytis character, extraordinary purity and precision despite concentration. Egon Müller Scharzhof TBA is among the world's most expensive wines by the bottle.

*Wine 11:* Tokaj, Hungary. Grape: Furmint (dominant) and Hárslevelű. Deep gold, botrytis-driven dried apricot, saffron, orange peel, volcanic mineral (Tokaj's andesite soils), high acid underlying the sweetness, savoury edge. 6 Puttonyos is the second-highest Aszu tier.

*Wine 12:* Niagara Peninsula, Ontario, Canada. Grape: Riesling. Frozen grape concentration (cryoextraction), pure primary fruit — lime/peach/apricot — with massive acid and sweetness simultaneously, very clean and precise without botrytis complexity. Icewine's hallmark is fruit purity; the Riesling adds aromatic lift.

**Part d) Sweetness mechanism, quality, and maturity — per wine**

*Wine 8 (Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise):* Mechanism — **Fortification (mutage)**: grape spirit added during fermentation to preserve natural grape sweetness (VDN/Vin Doux Naturel method). Quality: consistently high for the appellation; fresh and aromatic, best young (within 2-3 years of vintage). Maturity: young primary — the 2023 is at peak freshness; VDN Muscat does not typically benefit from long ageing.

*Wine 9 (Chambers Rutherglen Muscat):* Mechanism — **Fortification + fractional blending**: spirit addition stops fermentation; the wine is then blended across multiple years in a solera-like system and undergoes slow oxidative concentration in old casks exposed to the Rutherglen heat. Quality: extraordinary — one of the world's most concentrated wines. Maturity: the NV blend includes components decades old; currently at a peak-mature oxidative phase.

*Wine 10 (Egon Müller TBA):* Mechanism — **Botrytis cinerea (noble rot)**: selective harvesting of individually botrytized berries at extreme over-ripeness (Trockenbeerenauslese = "dried berry selection"); concentration through water loss and fungal action. Quality: the pinnacle of German sweet Riesling, globally ranked among the greatest wines in the world. Maturity: at 10 years, still primary-to-developing; genuine TBA can age for 50-100 years.

*Wine 11 (Royal Tokaji Aszú 6 Puttonyos):* Mechanism — **Botrytis maceration**: botrytized aszu berries (individually selected grapes that have shriveled and concentrated) are macerated as a paste in base wine or fermenting must; the resulting blend is fermented to completion, producing an intensely sweet, acid, and mineral wine. Quality: excellent — Royal Tokaji is one of the benchmark commercial Tokaji producers; 6 Puttonyos is near the top tier. Maturity: at 9 years, the 2017 is in its developing phase; primary fruit is integrating into secondary honey/saffron complexity. 20-40 years of development ahead.

*Wine 12 (Inniskillin Riesling Icewine):* Mechanism — **Cryoextraction (natural)**: grapes harvested frozen at -8°C or below; the ice crystals of water are left behind during pressing, concentrating juice sugars, acids, and aromas. No botrytis. Quality: high — Inniskillin is the brand that launched Canadian Icewine internationally; their Riesling bottling is precise and aromatic. Maturity: primary phase; Riesling Icewine can develop well for 10-15 years but is typically enjoyed young for its extraordinary primary fruit purity.

questions.modelAnswer:
## Question 1
**Wines 1-4 — same single grape variety, four countries**

---

#### Model Answer

**Part a) Identify the grape variety. (20 marks)**

STRONG SIGNAL: **Riesling.** The structure of the question — four wines, different origins, same single variety — points overwhelmingly to an internationally planted aromatic white. The most likely candidates are Riesling, Chardonnay, or Sauvignon Blanc. In the glass, the decisive cues are: very high acidity, no wood (reductive handling is typical), a taut linear frame, and the breadth of residual sugar variation across the four wines (one at 8.5% abv signals off-dry or sweeter production). Chardonnay at 8.5% would be structurally implausible without massive RS; Sauvignon Blanc at that alcohol does not occur in the dry-wine world. The combination of high acid, floral/aromatic perfume, slate/petrol development cues, and the range of RS confirms Riesling.

**Part b) Origin — per wine**

*Wine 1 — Joh. Jos. Prüm Wehlener Sonnenuhr Auslese, 2020, Mosel, Germany (8.5%)*
Low alcohol, residual sweetness (Auslese-level RS ~80-100 g/l), pronounced acidity, pale lemon gold, note of petrol/slate on the nose — STRONG SIGNAL: Mosel. The Mosel's distinctive light abv and the vineyard site (south-facing schist slopes) produce the characteristic racy, precise style. Smaragd/GG from Austria or Alsace Grand Cru would have higher alcohol and drier finish. Germany confirmed; Mosel most likely given the delicacy.

*Wine 2 — Weinbach Riesling Grand Cru Schlossberg, 2022, Alsace, France (13%)*
Higher alcohol (13%), bone dry or near-dry finish, full textural phenolic presence, spice, white peach, orange zest. STRONG SIGNAL: Alsace Grand Cru. The Schlossberg is a granite Grand Cru; its hallmark is power and grip without the oily weight of Mosel. The 13% abv and dry extract eliminate Mosel Auslese/Spatlese and point firmly to Alsace or possibly dry GG-Rheingau. The riper, more aromatic and textural profile with spice favors Alsace over Rheingau.

*Wine 3 — Grosset Polish Hill Riesling, 2024, Clare Valley, South Australia (12.5%)*
Bone dry, lime-cordial and lime zest, very high acidity, lean frame with almost no RS, medium-minus body, cool-climate clarity — STRONG SIGNAL: Clare or Eden Valley, South Australia. The signature lime and high acidity of the Clare Valley style is distinctive. Mosel at this dryness would show more slate/petrol with age; Alsace would be richer. New World acidity without the tropical ripeness of warmer zones: Clare Valley confirmed.

*Wine 4 — FX Pichler Ried Kellerberg Smaragd, 2021, Wachau, Austria (13.5%)*
Dry, powerful, stony mineral, peach and white blossom, phenolic grip and length, full body for a Riesling — STRONG SIGNAL: Wachau Smaragd or Rheingau GG. The Kellerberg is a gneiss site; expect a mineral stony character, weight and extract beyond Mosel or Clare Valley. Austria's Wachau is confirmed by the dry power and the specific granite/gneiss minerality distinct from Alsace's rounded spice or Clare's lime linearity.

**Part c) Quality and winemaking — per wine**

*Wine 1:* Top-quality Mosel Auslese from a legendary Prädikats producer. The 2020 was a warm vintage producing generous, complex wines; the Wehlener Sonnenuhr site adds concentration, floral lift, and slate-derived precision. Winemaking: reductive, cold fermentation, neutral stainless steel or large old wood, no malolactic, extended cellar rest. Quality: fine/wine tier, exceptional acid-to-sugar tension, outstanding potential 20+ year development arc.

*Wine 2:* Alsace Grand Cru from a historic biodynamic estate. Schlossberg granite gives linear mineral lift despite the ripeness. Winemaking: barrel fermentation possible (Weinbach uses large traditional foudres), spontaneous yeasts, no malo, extended ageing on lees. Quality: top tier, very long, complete, classic dry Alsace benchmark with genuine depth.

*Wine 3:* Grosset is one of Australia's most respected small producers; Polish Hill is their benchmark bottling from an estate vineyard in Clare Valley, with shallow shales, clay and gravel over ancient blue slate producing one of Australia's most structured dry Rieslings. Winemaking: stainless steel, cold fermentation, no oak, minimal SO2, reductive. Dry and focused. Quality: specialist premium, outstanding acid retention, 10-15 year aging trajectory for toasted lime complexity.

*Wine 4:* FX Pichler is an iconic Wachau Smaragd producer; Kellerberg is one of the great sites. The 2021 shows ripe fruit underpinned by stony precision. Winemaking: extended maceration possible, cold fermentation, stainless steel, Smaragd classification (ripest harvest category). Quality: fine-wine tier, one of Austria's most age-worthy dry Riesling styles.

---

### Question 2
**Wines 5-7 — same variety, same country (Loire Valley SB), quality calibration**

**Parts a) Grape variety and country (15 marks)**

STRONG SIGNAL: **Sauvignon Blanc, France.** The stem says "same grape variety, same country" which in the P1 tree strongly favors Sauvignon Blanc (Loire France) or Chardonnay (Burgundy France). *Country:* France.

**Part b) Specific origin — per wine**

*Wine 5 — Sancerre Les Romains, Henri Bourgeois, 2024:* Sancerre is the most famous Loire SB appellation; the Les Romains vineyard is a flint-and-limestone south-facing slope producing the most concentrated, flinty-mineral style. Sancerre often shows a smoky, almost gunflint lift above simpler fruity SB. Quality is the highest of this trio; the 2024 vintage was warm and concentrated.

*Wine 6 — Menetou-Salon Les Bornés, Domaine de Chasseignes, 2024:* Menetou-Salon is the adjacent satellite appellation of Sancerre, producing very similar limestone-dominant Sauvignon Blanc at a slightly lower quality ceiling and significantly lower price. This is the mid-tier regional benchmark: similar aromatics to Sancerre but slightly less complexity, intensity, and aging potential.

*Wine 7 — Pouilly-Fumé Les Berthiers, Jean-Claude Dagueneau, 2023:* Pouilly-Fumé sits across the Loire from Sancerre on similar Kimmeridgian and silex soils. The Dagueneau family (Didier Dagueneau's heirs) is the prestige producer in the appellation. Les Berthiers is their classic cuvée. Quality here competes with top Sancerre; the style tends slightly fuller and rounder than Sancerre due to silex soil character.

**Part c) Quality ranking (24 marks)**

Ranking: Wine 7 (Pouilly-Fumé Dagueneau) = Wine 5 (Sancerre Bourgeois) > Wine 6 (Menetou-Salon).

*Justification:* Wine 7 (Pouilly-Fumé Dagueneau) and Wine 5 (Sancerre Bourgeois Les Romains) are peer-quality wines at the top of Loire SB's quality hierarchy. Dagueneau's prestige within Pouilly-Fumé is analogous to Bourgeois' single-vineyard status in Sancerre; both show great mineral complexity, laser-precise acidity, and aging capacity. Wine 6 (Menetou-Salon) is genuine but shows somewhat simpler aromatic profile, less concentration, and a shorter palate — appropriate for its regional tier.

*Production note:* Production is broadly similar across the flight: cool fermentation to preserve Sauvignon Blanc aromatics, no malolactic conversion, no overt new oak, and possible older foudre or extended lees texture in the top Sancerre/Pouilly-Fumé cuvées. This is not primarily a winemaking-contrast question; the quality ranking rests on site quality, vine age, producer level, concentration, length, and regional hierarchy.

**Part d) Commercial positioning — per wine**

*Wine 5 (Sancerre):* Globally recognized appellation; premium restaurant by-the-glass and retail market; £20-35 retail; positioned as the world standard for crisp dry white. Excellent commercial reach into fine dining, wine trade, and direct consumer channels.

*Wine 6 (Menetou-Salon):* Under-the-radar "value Sancerre" positioning; £14-20; appeals to on-trade buyers and educated consumers seeking Sancerre-equivalent quality at lower price. Strong sommelier-facing commercial position.

*Wine 7 (Pouilly-Fumé Dagueneau):* Prestige benchmark; £30-60+ for flagship cuvées; positions as one of the world's great dry whites, competing with premium Burgundy in top restaurants and collector markets. Commercial reach is narrower but at higher margin.

### Question 3
**Wines 8-10 — same country (Alsace, France), three different single varieties**

Medium-deep golden color, waxy, pear, ginger, dried apricot, honey, broad and full-bodied, lower acid than Riesling, textural richness, long. STRONG SIGNAL: Pinot Gris, Alsace. The weight, aromatic warmth, and ginger-apricot character are signature. 14% abv confirms the richness of Alsace production at this Grand Cru/site level. Origin: Alsace, France; variety: Pinot Gris.

*Wine 9 — Zind-Humbrecht Gewurztraminer Clos Windsbuhl, 2021, Alsace, France (14.5%):*
Deep gold, exotic rose petal, lychee, ginger, Turkish delight, very aromatic, broad low-acid palate, almost oily texture, high alcohol. STRONG SIGNAL: Gewurztraminer. This is the most aromatically distinctive variety in the world; misidentification is unlikely if the candidate recognizes the lychee-rose-ginger trinity. *Wine 10 — Zind-Humbrecht Muscat Goldert Grand Cru, 2022, Alsace, France (14%):*
Pale gold, fresh grape, orange blossom, musk, exotic but lighter than Gewurztraminer, high aromatic intensity but more delicate, off-dry or dry finish. STRONG SIGNAL: Muscat. Muscat's hallmark is the grape/orange blossom aromatics at a lighter body than Gewurztraminer. The Goldert Grand Cru is a volcanic (basalt) site that gives Muscat unusual mineral grip. Origin: Alsace, France; variety: Muscat.

**Part b) Method of production — per wine**

All three wines are produced under the fundamental Alsace model: single-variety labelling, traditional free-run pressing, long cold settling, fermentation in large neutral foudres or stainless steel (Burn uses both; ZH uses large foudres), minimal sulphur, low-temperature slow fermentation to preserve aromatics, no malolactic fermentation, extended lees ageing. The key differentiators by variety: Gewurztraminer may be given partial skin contact to build texture; Pinot Gris may receive slightly later picking for maximum richness; Muscat requires meticulous temperature control to preserve delicate florals. *Wine 9 (Gewurztraminer):* High quality; the Clos Windsbuhl site gives Gewurztraminer unusual restraint for the variety, avoiding the flabbiness that can afflict lower-tier examples. Still primary in 2021; will develop greater aromatic integration and phenolic polish over 8-12 years. Commercial: appeals strongly to fine-dining, Asian cuisine markets, and collectors of Alsace rarities.

*Wine 10 (Muscat):* Very high quality but most immediately approachable of the three; Muscat ages well at Grand Cru level but its primary appeal is the brilliant fresh-grape aromatic intensity. Goldert's mineral character adds structural longevity. Current phase: primary/youthful; likely best 2024-2030. Commercial: harder sell globally due to Muscat's perceived "sweet/simple" association; rewards educated buyers who understand dry Alsace Muscat.

### Question 4
**Wines 11-12 — same variety (Chenin Blanc), same region (Vouvray), two development stages**

---

#### Model Answer

**Part a) Grape variety and region (20 marks)**

STRONG SIGNAL: **Chenin Blanc, Vouvray, Loire Valley, France.** The stem — same variety, same region, implied comparison across development stages — strongly suggests a variety with outstanding aging potential from a classic, hierarchically structured region. In France, this points first to Burgundy Chardonnay (same region, different cuvées) or Loire Chenin Blanc. The presence of a demi-sec version (Wine 12) narrows immediately: Chardonnay does not appear as a demi-sec in French appellations; Chenin Blanc from Vouvray does regularly. Vouvray produces the full dry-to-sweet-to-sparkling Chenin spectrum from a single appellation, giving the examiner complete flexibility to contrast two development states in one question.

Variety: Chenin Blanc.
Region: Vouvray, Loire Valley, France.

**Part b) Maturity and natural vs human factors — per wine**

*Wine 11 — Vouvray Le Mont Sec, Domaine Huet, 2023 (12.5%):*
Stage of maturity: young, primary. The 2023 vintage is a very recent vintage for Vouvray; the wine is currently showing primary fruit aromas (quince, green apple, fresh hay) and has not begun the secondary development that characterizes mature Huet Vouvray. The high acidity from Chenin is prominent and almost austere. Time in bottle: ~1-2 years; full maturity expected in 5-15 years.

Natural factors: the tuffeau limestone soils of the Le Mont vineyard impart freshness and mineral precision. The 2023 vintage was warm but Vouvray's Atlantic-moderated climate preserved the characteristic acidity. Human factors: Huet is a benchmark biodynamic estate; minimal intervention, ambient yeast fermentation, extended lees ageing, traditional demi-muid or foudre use. Sec classification (dry) reflects harvest decisions at lower potential alcohol. The balance in the 2023 sec is natural factor-led: site and vintage shaped the wine's linearity.

*Wine 12 — Vouvray Le Mont Demi-Sec, Domaine Huet, 2015 (12.5%):*
Stage of maturity: developing, approaching the early tertiary phase. The 2015 vintage was warm and concentrated; at eleven years, the demi-sec has begun to develop secondary complexity — lanolin, toasted quince, honeycomb, emerging petrol notes on the nose, with the RS integrating into the mid-palate rather than appearing raw or sweet. Still has decades ahead.

Natural factors: the Le Mont site again (same vineyard), with the 2015 vintage's warmth contributing more phenolic richness and residual sugar. Human factors: the demi-sec classification reflects harvest decisions to leave more natural sugars (achieved through longer hang-time rather than botrytis); the residual sugar (~18-25 g/l typical for Vouvray demi-sec) is a deliberate human choice. The winemaking (same biodynamic regime as Wine 11) means the difference between the two wines reflects primarily vintage and harvest-time decision-making.

Relative importance of natural vs human: Wine 11 (sec, 2023) is more clearly natural-factor-driven in its primary linear austerity; Wine 12 (demi-sec, 2015) shows human harvest-timing decisions producing a richer, rounder style that, with bottle time, has moved toward a secondary complexity both wines ultimately share.

STRONG SIGNAL: **Madeira, Portugal.** The stem — same region, same producer, four wines — in P3 with a fortified/oxidative profile most logically points to Madeira, Sherry (Jerez), or Port. The decisive in-glass evidence for Madeira: extremely high acidity unlike Sherry or Port, volatile aromatics (curry/nuts/caramel), the characteristic tangy finish, and the extraordinary longevity that makes it the most age-resilient wine in the world. The four wines span dry to sweet (Sercial to Malmsey — the classic Madeira gradient), which is a structure uniquely available from Madeira's four main grape varieties. Sherry's same-region same-producer question would span Fino/Amontillado/Oloroso/PX — possible but the acid architecture is different.

Region: Madeira.

**Part b) Winemaking comparison across four wines (20 marks)**

All four wines share the fundamental Madeira production framework: Vitis vinifera grapes harvested from the island's steep terraces; fermentation stopped by fortification (grape spirit addition at different stages of fermentation to achieve the appropriate RS level per variety); estufagem (heating process, either in tanks — canteiro system or industrial estufa) or canteiro maturation (ageing in old barrels in warm loft spaces — the premium method used by these producers for 10+ year wines); oxidative maturation in used barrique or old casks; and eventual bottling under NV designation after meeting minimum age statement criteria.

Key differences by style:
- *Sercial (dry):* fermentation continues to near-dryness before fortification; highest acid of the four; aged for minimum 10 years in the canteiro (barrel in warm loft) system; pale amber gold; driest finish (often <10 g/l RS effectively).
- *Verdelho (medium-dry):* fermentation stopped slightly earlier than Sercial; slightly more RS (~20-40 g/l); broader and nuttier than Sercial but still marked by Madeira's characteristic high acid.
- *Bual (medium-sweet):* fermentation stopped with moderate sweetness (~60-90 g/l RS); deeper amber color; richer, with more dried fig and caramel notes; still very high acid.
- *Malmsey (sweet):* fermentation stopped earliest — highest RS (~90-150 g/l); deepest color; most opulent, most sweet, most accessible to non-specialist consumers; the Madeira "gateway" variety.

The canteiro system (used for premium 10- and 15-year age statements) ages the wines in warm loft spaces where natural summer heat drives the estufagem, producing a more complex, less aggressive result than industrial estufa tanks.

**Part b) Winemaking comparison across four wines (20 marks)**

All four wines share the fundamental Madeira production framework: Vitis vinifera grapes harvested from the island's steep terraces; fermentation stopped by fortification (grape spirit addition at different stages of fermentation to achieve the appropriate RS level per variety); estufagem (heating process, either in tanks — canteiro system or industrial estufa) or canteiro maturation (ageing in old barrels in warm loft spaces — the premium method used by these producers for 10+ year wines); oxidative maturation in used barrique or old casks; and eventual bottling under NV designation after meeting minimum age statement criteria.

Key differences by style:
- *Sercial (dry):* fermentation continues to near-dryness before fortification; highest acid of the four; aged for minimum 10 years in the canteiro (barrel in warm loft) system; pale amber gold; driest finish (often <10 g/l RS effectively).
- *Verdelho (medium-dry):* fermentation stopped slightly earlier than Sercial; slightly more RS (~20-40 g/l); broader and nuttier than Sercial but still marked by Madeira's characteristic high acid.
- *Bual (medium-sweet):* fermentation stopped with moderate sweetness (~60-90 g/l RS); deeper amber color; richer, with more dried fig and caramel notes; still very high acid.
- *Malmsey (sweet):* fermentation stopped earliest — highest RS (~90-150 g/l); deepest color; most opulent, most sweet, most accessible to non-specialist consumers; the Madeira "gateway" variety.

The canteiro system (used for premium 10- and 15-year age statements) ages the wines in warm loft spaces where natural summer heat drives the estufagem, producing a more complex, less aggressive result than industrial estufa tanks.

### Question 3
**Wines 8-12 — five countries, residual sugar question**

---

#### Model Answer

**Part a) Residual sugar — per wine**

*Wine 8 (Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, 2023):* Approximately 100-120 g/l RS. Fortified VDN (Vin Doux Naturel), Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. ABV 15%.

*Wine 9 (Chambers Muscat Liqueur NV, Rutherglen):* Approximately 300-400 g/l RS (Rutherglen Muscat is one of the world's richest sweet wines). ABV 17.5%.

*Wine 10 (Egon Müller TBA, 2016, Mosel):* Approximately 400-500 g/l RS (TBA is among the sweetest unfortified wines). ABV ~7%.

*Wine 11 (Royal Tokaji Aszú 6 Puttonyos, 2017):* Approximately 150-180 g/l RS minimum (6 Puttonyos regulatory minimum is 150 g/l). ABV ~10.5%.

*Wine 12 (Inniskillin Riesling Icewine, 2022, Niagara):* Approximately 180-220 g/l RS. ABV ~9%.

**Part b) Alcohol levels — per wine**

As stated on the wine labels: Wine 8 = 15%; Wine 9 = 17.5%; Wine 10 = 7%; Wine 11 = 10.5%; Wine 12 = 9%.

**Part c) Origin and variety — per wine**

*Wine 8:* Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise (VDN), Rhône Valley, France. Grape: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. Bright aromatic orange blossom, lychee, fresh grape, medium gold color, sweet and fragrant but not as concentrated as Australian Muscat.

*Wine 9:* Rutherglen, Victoria, Australia. Grape: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains (Rutherglen Muscat). Deep amber-brown, extraordinarily concentrated raisin/coffee/Christmas cake/treacle aromas, extraordinary viscosity. Rutherglen Muscat is produced by the solera-like fractional blending system over decades.

*Wine 10:* Mosel, Germany. Grape: Riesling. Extremely high acid even with the enormous sweetness, peach/apricot/honey/noble rot botrytis character, extraordinary purity and precision despite concentration. Egon Müller Scharzhof TBA is among the world's most expensive wines by the bottle.

*Wine 11:* Tokaj, Hungary. Grape: Furmint (dominant) and Hárslevelű. Deep gold, botrytis-driven dried apricot, saffron, orange peel, volcanic mineral (Tokaj's andesite soils), high acid underlying the sweetness, savoury edge. 6 Puttonyos is the second-highest Aszu tier.

*Wine 12:* Niagara Peninsula, Ontario, Canada. Grape: Riesling. Frozen grape concentration (cryoextraction), pure primary fruit — lime/peach/apricot — with massive acid and sweetness simultaneously, very clean and precise without botrytis complexity. Icewine's hallmark is fruit purity; the Riesling adds aromatic lift.

**Part d) Sweetness mechanism, quality, and maturity — per wine**

*Wine 8 (Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise):* Mechanism — **Fortification (mutage)**: grape spirit added during fermentation to preserve natural grape sweetness (VDN/Vin Doux Naturel method). Quality: consistently high for the appellation; fresh and aromatic, best young (within 2-3 years of vintage). Maturity: young primary — the 2023 is at peak freshness; VDN Muscat does not typically benefit from long ageing.

*Wine 9 (Chambers Rutherglen Muscat):* Mechanism — **Fortification + fractional blending**: spirit addition stops fermentation; the wine is then blended across multiple years in a solera-like system and undergoes slow oxidative concentration in old casks exposed to the Rutherglen heat. Quality: extraordinary — one of the world's most concentrated wines. Maturity: the NV blend includes components decades old; currently at a peak-mature oxidative phase.

*Wine 10 (Egon Müller TBA):* Mechanism — **Botrytis cinerea (noble rot)**: selective harvesting of individually botrytized berries at extreme over-ripeness (Trockenbeerenauslese = "dried berry selection"); concentration through water loss and fungal action. Quality: the pinnacle of German sweet Riesling, globally ranked among the greatest wines in the world. Maturity: at 10 years, still primary-to-developing; genuine TBA can age for 50-100 years.

*Wine 11 (Royal Tokaji Aszú 6 Puttonyos):* Mechanism — **Botrytis maceration**: botrytized aszu berries (individually selected grapes that have shriveled and concentrated) are macerated as a paste in base wine or fermenting must; the resulting blend is fermented to completion, producing an intensely sweet, acid, and mineral wine. Quality: excellent — Royal Tokaji is one of the benchmark commercial Tokaji producers; 6 Puttonyos is near the top tier. Maturity: at 9 years, the 2017 is in its developing phase; primary fruit is integrating into secondary honey/saffron complexity. 20-40 years of development ahead.

*Wine 12 (Inniskillin Riesling Icewine):* Mechanism — **Cryoextraction (natural)**: grapes harvested frozen at -8°C or below; the ice crystals of water are left behind during pressing, concentrating juice sugars, acids, and aromas. No botrytis. Quality: high — Inniskillin is the brand that launched Canadian Icewine internationally; their Riesling bottling is precise and aromatic. Maturity: primary phase; Riesling Icewine can develop well for 10-15 years but is typically enjoyed young for its extraordinary primary fruit purity.

**Part b) Specific origin — per wine**

*Wine 5 — Sancerre Les Romains, Henri Bourgeois, 2024:* Sancerre is the most famous Loire SB appellation; the Les Romains vineyard is a flint-and-limestone south-facing slope producing the most concentrated, flinty-mineral style. Sancerre often shows a smoky, almost gunflint lift above simpler fruity SB. Quality is the highest of this trio; the 2024 vintage was warm and concentrated.

*Wine 6 — Menetou-Salon Les Bornés, Domaine de Chasseignes, 2024:* Menetou-Salon is the adjacent satellite appellation of Sancerre, producing very similar limestone-dominant Sauvignon Blanc at a slightly lower quality ceiling and significantly lower price. This is the mid-tier regional benchmark: similar aromatics to Sancerre but slightly less complexity, intensity, and aging potential.

*Wine 7 — Pouilly-Fumé Les Berthiers, Jean-Claude Dagueneau, 2023:* Pouilly-Fumé sits across the Loire from Sancerre on similar Kimmeridgian and silex soils. The Dagueneau family (Didier Dagueneau's heirs) is the prestige producer in the appellation. Les Berthiers is their classic cuvée. Quality here competes with top Sancerre; the style tends slightly fuller and rounder than Sancerre due to silex soil character.

Pale gold, fresh grape, orange blossom, musk, exotic but lighter than Gewurztraminer, high aromatic intensity but more delicate, off-dry or dry finish. STRONG SIGNAL: Muscat. All three wines are produced under the fundamental Alsace model: single-variety labelling, traditional free-run pressing, long cold settling, fermentation in large neutral foudres or stainless steel (Burn uses both; ZH uses large foudres), minimal sulphur, low-temperature slow fermentation to preserve aromatics, no malolactic fermentation, extended lees ageing. *Wine 8 (Pinot Gris):* High quality; full-bodied, ageworthy, currently in its primary-to-developing phase (2022 is still young). Potential 10-15 years of development toward petrol, walnut, and mature dried fruit character. Style: serious and contemplative rather than immediately approachable; pairs with rich food (charcuterie, game, foie gras).

*Wine 9 (Gewurztraminer):* High quality; the Clos Windsbuhl site gives Gewurztraminer unusual restraint for the variety, avoiding the flabbiness that can afflict lower-tier examples. Still primary in 2021; will develop greater aromatic integration and phenolic polish over 8-12 years. Commercial: appeals strongly to fine-dining, Asian cuisine markets, and collectors of Alsace rarities.

*Wine 10 (Muscat):* Very high quality but most immediately approachable of the three; Muscat ages well at Grand Cru level but its primary appeal is the brilliant fresh-grape aromatic intensity. Commercial: harder sell globally due to Muscat's perceived "sweet/simple" association; rewards educated buyers who understand dry Alsace Muscat.

Base varieties: Xarel-lo, Macabeo, Parellada (native Catalan varieties).

*Wine 3 (Nyetimber):* Traditional method: secondary fermentation in bottle; sur-lattes ageing minimum; riddling and disgorgement at Nyetimber (typically 3+ years for NV). The hallmark of English sparkling production is maximizing natural acid retention from the cool climate, with controlled MLF to soften the most austere examples.

**Part c) Quality and commercial positioning — per wine**

*Wine 2 (Cava Gran Reserva):* Quality: very high. Gramona III Lustros is one of Cava's most ambitious wines, competing with prestige Champagne on complexity. ### Question 2
**Wines 4-7 — same region, same producer (Madeira, four styles)**

---

#### Model Answer

**Part a) Region (15 marks)**

STRONG SIGNAL: **Madeira, Portugal.** The stem — same region, same producer, four wines — in P3 with a fortified/oxidative profile most logically points to Madeira, Sherry (Jerez), or Port. The decisive in-glass evidence for Madeira: extremely high acidity unlike Sherry or Port, volatile aromatics (curry/nuts/caramel), the characteristic tangy finish, and the extraordinary longevity that makes it the most age-resilient wine in the world. The four wines span dry to sweet (Sercial to Malmsey — the classic Madeira gradient), which is a structure uniquely available from Madeira's four main grape varieties. Sherry's same-region same-producer question would span Fino/Amontillado/Oloroso/PX — possible but the acid architecture is different.

Region: Madeira.

**Part b) Winemaking comparison across four wines (20 marks)**

All four wines share the fundamental Madeira production framework: Vitis vinifera grapes harvested from the island's steep terraces; fermentation stopped by fortification (grape spirit addition at different stages of fermentation to achieve the appropriate RS level per variety); estufagem (heating process, either in tanks — canteiro system or industrial estufa) or canteiro maturation (ageing in old barrels in warm loft spaces — the premium method used by these producers for 10+ year wines); oxidative maturation in used barrique or old casks; and eventual bottling under NV designation after meeting minimum age statement criteria.

Key differences by style:
- *Sercial (dry):* fermentation continues to near-dryness before fortification; highest acid of the four; aged for minimum 10 years in the canteiro (barrel in warm loft) system; pale amber gold; driest finish (often <10 g/l RS effectively).
- *Verdelho (medium-dry):* fermentation stopped slightly earlier than Sercial; slightly more RS (~20-40 g/l); broader and nuttier than Sercial but still marked by Madeira's characteristic high acid.
- *Bual (medium-sweet):* fermentation stopped with moderate sweetness (~60-90 g/l RS); deeper amber color; richer, with more dried fig and caramel notes; still very high acid.
- *Malmsey (sweet):* fermentation stopped earliest — highest RS (~90-150 g/l); deepest color; most opulent, most sweet, most accessible to non-specialist consumers; the Madeira "gateway" variety.

The canteiro system (used for premium 10- and 15-year age statements) ages the wines in warm loft spaces where natural summer heat drives the estufagem, producing a more complex, less aggressive result than industrial estufa tanks.

**Part c) Quality, style, and commercial appeal — per wine**

*Wine 4 (Sercial 10 Year Old, Henriques & Henriques):* Excellent quality. Sercial is the most intellectually demanding Madeira for non-specialists — very high acid, almond/curry/sea-salt nose, bone-dry tangy finish. Commercial: appeals strongly to the wine trade, top sommeliers, and aperitif/food-pairing contexts (matches smoked fish, charcuterie, aged cheeses). Limited mass market. £20-35.

*Wine 5 (Verdelho 15 Year Old, Henriques & Henriques):* Excellent quality; the 15-year age statement adds complexity over the 10-year Sercial. Verdelho's slightly sweeter profile bridges the dry-sweet spectrum. Commercial: slightly broader appeal than Sercial; good food pairing versatility; appreciated by consumers who find Sercial too austere. £25-45.

*Wine 6 (Bual 10 Year Old, Blandy's):* Very good quality. Bual sits in the premium sweet-wine conversation — high enough acid to avoid cloying sweetness, concentrated dried fruit and caramel character. Commercial: strong fine-wine market positioning alongside dessert service; £25-40. Blandy's is arguably the most internationally recognized Madeira brand.

*Wine 7 (Malmsey 15 Year Old, Blandy's):* Exceptional quality; the 15-year age statement on the sweetest style produces extraordinary complexity — dried figs, coffee, chocolate, marmalade, with Madeira's signature tangy acid preventing heaviness. Commercial: most accessible Madeira style to new consumers; strong in gift, dessert, and cocktail markets; £40-70.

**Wines 4-7 — same region, same producer (Madeira, four styles)**

The four wines span dry to sweet (Sercial to Malmsey — the classic Madeira gradient), which is a structure uniquely available from Madeira's four main grape varieties. Sherry's same-region same-producer question would span Fino/Amontillado/Oloroso/PX — possible but the acid architecture is different.

**Part b) Winemaking comparison across four wines (20 marks)**

All four wines share the fundamental Madeira production framework: Vitis vinifera grapes harvested from the island's steep terraces; fermentation stopped by fortification (grape spirit addition at different stages of fermentation to achieve the appropriate RS level per variety); estufagem (heating process, either in tanks — canteiro system or industrial estufa) or canteiro maturation (ageing in old barrels in warm loft spaces — the premium method used by these producers for 10+ year wines); oxidative maturation in used barrique or old casks; and eventual bottling under NV designation after meeting minimum age statement criteria.

Key differences by style:
- *Sercial (dry):* fermentation continues to near-dryness before fortification; highest acid of the four; aged for minimum 10 years in the canteiro (barrel in warm loft) system; pale amber gold; driest finish (often <10 g/l RS effectively).
- *Verdelho (medium-dry):* fermentation stopped slightly earlier than Sercial; slightly more RS (~20-40 g/l); broader and nuttier than Sercial but still marked by Madeira's characteristic high acid.
- *Bual (medium-sweet):* fermentation stopped with moderate sweetness (~60-90 g/l RS); deeper amber color; richer, with more dried fig and caramel notes; still very high acid.
- *Malmsey (sweet):* fermentation stopped earliest — highest RS (~90-150 g/l); deepest color; most opulent, most sweet, most accessible to non-specialist consumers; the Madeira "gateway" variety.

The canteiro system (used for premium 10- and 15-year age statements) ages the wines in warm loft spaces where natural summer heat drives the estufagem, producing a more complex, less aggressive result than industrial estufa tanks.

**Part c) Quality, style, and commercial appeal — per wine**

*Wine 4 (Sercial 10 Year Old, Henriques & Henriques):* Excellent quality. Sercial is the most intellectually demanding Madeira for non-specialists — very high acid, almond/curry/sea-salt nose, bone-dry tangy finish. Commercial: appeals strongly to the wine trade, top sommeliers, and aperitif/food-pairing contexts (matches smoked fish, charcuterie, aged cheeses). Limited mass market. £20-35.

*Wine 5 (Verdelho 15 Year Old, Henriques & Henriques):* Excellent quality; the 15-year age statement adds complexity over the 10-year Sercial. Verdelho's slightly sweeter profile bridges the dry-sweet spectrum. Commercial: slightly broader appeal than Sercial; good food pairing versatility; appreciated by consumers who find Sercial too austere. £25-45.

*Wine 6 (Bual 10 Year Old, Blandy's):* Very good quality. Bual sits in the premium sweet-wine conversation — high enough acid to avoid cloying sweetness, concentrated dried fruit and caramel character. Commercial: strong fine-wine market positioning alongside dessert service; £25-40. Blandy's is arguably the most internationally recognized Madeira brand.

*Wine 7 (Malmsey 15 Year Old, Blandy's):* Exceptional quality; the 15-year age statement on the sweetest style produces extraordinary complexity — dried figs, coffee, chocolate, marmalade, with Madeira's signature tangy acid preventing heaviness. Commercial: most accessible Madeira style to new consumers; strong in gift, dessert, and cocktail markets; £40-70.

**Wines 8-12 — five countries, residual sugar question**

#### Model Answer

**Part a) Residual sugar — per wine**

*Wine 8 (Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise, 2023):* Approximately 100-120 g/l RS. Fortified VDN (Vin Doux Naturel), Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. ABV 15%.

*Wine 11 (Royal Tokaji Aszú 6 Puttonyos, 2017):* Approximately 150-180 g/l RS minimum (6 Puttonyos regulatory minimum is 150 g/l). ABV ~10.5%.

*Wine 12 (Inniskillin Riesling Icewine, 2022, Niagara):* Approximately 180-220 g/l RS. ABV ~9%.

**Part b) Alcohol levels — per wine**

As stated on the wine labels: Wine 8 = 15%; Wine 9 = 17.5%; Wine 10 = 7%; Wine 11 = 10.5%; Wine 12 = 9%.

**Part c) Origin and variety — per wine**

*Wine 8:* Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise (VDN), Rhône Valley, France. Grape: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains. Bright aromatic orange blossom, lychee, fresh grape, medium gold color, sweet and fragrant but not as concentrated as Australian Muscat.

*Wine 9:* Rutherglen, Victoria, Australia. Grape: Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains (Rutherglen Muscat). Deep amber-brown, extraordinarily concentrated raisin/coffee/Christmas cake/treacle aromas, extraordinary viscosity. Rutherglen Muscat is produced by the solera-like fractional blending system over decades.

*Wine 10:* Mosel, Germany. Grape: Riesling. Extremely high acid even with the enormous sweetness, peach/apricot/honey/noble rot botrytis character, extraordinary purity and precision despite concentration. Egon Müller Scharzhof TBA is among the world's most expensive wines by the bottle.

*Wine 11:* Tokaj, Hungary. Grape: Furmint (dominant) and Hárslevelű. Deep gold, botrytis-driven dried apricot, saffron, orange peel, volcanic mineral (Tokaj's andesite soils), high acid underlying the sweetness, savoury edge. 6 Puttonyos is the second-highest Aszu tier.

*Wine 12:* Niagara Peninsula, Ontario, Canada. Grape: Riesling. Frozen grape concentration (cryoextraction), pure primary fruit — lime/peach/apricot — with massive acid and sweetness simultaneously, very clean and precise without botrytis complexity. Icewine's hallmark is fruit purity; the Riesling adds aromatic lift.

**Part d) Sweetness mechanism, quality, and maturity — per wine**

*Wine 8 (Muscat de Beaumes-de-Venise):* Mechanism — **Fortification (mutage)**: grape spirit added during fermentation to preserve natural grape sweetness (VDN/Vin Doux Naturel method). Quality: consistently high for the appellation; fresh and aromatic, best young (within 2-3 years of vintage). Maturity: young primary — the 2023 is at peak freshness; VDN Muscat does not typically benefit from long ageing.

*Wine 9 (Chambers Rutherglen Muscat):* Mechanism — **Fortification + fractional blending**: spirit addition stops fermentation; the wine is then blended across multiple years in a solera-like system and undergoes slow oxidative concentration in old casks exposed to the Rutherglen heat. Quality: extraordinary — one of the world's most concentrated wines. Maturity: the NV blend includes components decades old; currently at a peak-mature oxidative phase.

*Wine 10 (Egon Müller TBA):* Mechanism — **Botrytis cinerea (noble rot)**: selective harvesting of individually botrytized berries at extreme over-ripeness (Trockenbeerenauslese = "dried berry selection"); concentration through water loss and fungal action. Quality: the pinnacle of German sweet Riesling, globally ranked among the greatest wines in the world. Maturity: at 10 years, still primary-to-developing; genuine TBA can age for 50-100 years.

*Wine 11 (Royal Tokaji Aszú 6 Puttonyos):* Mechanism — **Botrytis maceration**: botrytized aszu berries (individually selected grapes that have shriveled and concentrated) are macerated as a paste in base wine or fermenting must; the resulting blend is fermented to completion, producing an intensely sweet, acid, and mineral wine. Quality: excellent — Royal Tokaji is one of the benchmark commercial Tokaji producers; 6 Puttonyos is near the top tier. Maturity: at 9 years, the 2017 is in its developing phase; primary fruit is integrating into secondary honey/saffron complexity. 20-40 years of development ahead.

*Wine 12 (Inniskillin Riesling Icewine):* Mechanism — **Cryoextraction (natural)**: grapes harvested frozen at -8°C or below; the ice crystals of water are left behind during pressing, concentrating juice sugars, acids, and aromas. No botrytis. Quality: high — Inniskillin is the brand that launched Canadian Icewine internationally; their Riesling bottling is precise and aromatic. Maturity: primary phase; Riesling Icewine can develop well for 10-15 years but is typically enjoyed young for its extraordinary primary fruit purity.

## Question 3
**Wines 8-10 — same country (Alsace, France), three different single varieties**

---

#### Model Answer

**Part a) Variety and origin — per wine**

*Wine 8 — Ernest Burn Pinot Gris Terre Brune, 2022, Alsace, France (14%):*
Medium-deep golden color, waxy, pear, ginger, dried apricot, honey, broad and full-bodied, lower acid than Riesling, textural richness, long. STRONG SIGNAL: Pinot Gris, Alsace. The weight, aromatic warmth, and ginger-apricot character are signature. 14% abv confirms the richness of Alsace production at this Grand Cru/site level. Origin: Alsace, France; variety: Pinot Gris.

*Wine 9 — Zind-Humbrecht Gewurztraminer Clos Windsbuhl, 2021, Alsace, France (14.5%):*
Deep gold, exotic rose petal, lychee, ginger, Turkish delight, very aromatic, broad low-acid palate, almost oily texture, high alcohol. STRONG SIGNAL: Gewurztraminer. This is the most aromatically distinctive variety in the world; misidentification is unlikely if the candidate recognizes the lychee-rose-ginger trinity. Clos Windsbuhl is a monopole limestone site from Zind-Humbrecht, one of the prestige Alsace houses. Origin: Alsace, France; variety: Gewurztraminer.

*Wine 10 — Zind-Humbrecht Muscat Goldert Grand Cru, 2022, Alsace, France (14%):*
Pale gold, fresh grape, orange blossom, musk, exotic but lighter than Gewurztraminer, high aromatic intensity but more delicate, off-dry or dry finish. STRONG SIGNAL: Muscat. Muscat's hallmark is the grape/orange blossom aromatics at a lighter body than Gewurztraminer. The Goldert Grand Cru is a volcanic (basalt) site that gives Muscat unusual mineral grip. Origin: Alsace, France; variety: Muscat.

**Part b) Method of production — per wine**

All three wines are produced under the fundamental Alsace model: single-variety labelling, traditional free-run pressing, long cold settling, fermentation in large neutral foudres or stainless steel (Burn uses both; ZH uses large foudres), minimal sulphur, low-temperature slow fermentation to preserve aromatics, no malolactic fermentation, extended lees ageing. The key differentiators by variety: Gewurztraminer may be given partial skin contact to build texture; Pinot Gris may receive slightly later picking for maximum richness; Muscat requires meticulous temperature control to preserve delicate florals. Grand Cru status for Wines 9 and 10 implies lower yields and selective harvesting.

**Part c) Quality, style, and development potential — per wine**

*Wine 8 (Pinot Gris):* High quality; full-bodied, ageworthy, currently in its primary-to-developing phase (2022 is still young). Potential 10-15 years of development toward petrol, walnut, and mature dried fruit character. Style: serious and contemplative rather than immediately approachable; pairs with rich food (charcuterie, game, foie gras).

*Wine 9 (Gewurztraminer):* High quality; the Clos Windsbuhl site gives Gewurztraminer unusual restraint for the variety, avoiding the flabbiness that can afflict lower-tier examples. **Part b) Winemaking comparison across four wines (20 marks)**

All four wines share the fundamental Madeira production framework: Vitis vinifera grapes harvested from the island's steep terraces; fermentation stopped by fortification (grape spirit addition at different stages of fermentation to achieve the appropriate RS level per variety); estufagem (heating process, either in tanks — canteiro system or industrial estufa) or canteiro maturation (ageing in old barrels in warm loft spaces — the premium method used by these producers for 10+ year wines); oxidative maturation in used barrique or old casks; and eventual bottling under NV designation after meeting minimum age statement criteria.

Key differences by style:
- *Sercial (dry):* fermentation continues to near-dryness before fortification; highest acid of the four; aged for minimum 10 years in the canteiro (barrel in warm loft) system; pale amber gold; driest finish (often <10 g/l RS effectively).
- *Verdelho (medium-dry):* fermentation stopped slightly earlier than Sercial; slightly more RS (~20-40 g/l); broader and nuttier than Sercial but still marked by Madeira's characteristic high acid.
- *Bual (medium-sweet):* fermentation stopped with moderate sweetness (~60-90 g/l RS); deeper amber color; richer, with more dried fig and caramel notes; still very high acid.
- *Malmsey (sweet):* fermentation stopped earliest — highest RS (~90-150 g/l); deepest color; most opulent, most sweet, most accessible to non-specialist consumers; the Madeira "gateway" variety.

The canteiro system (used for premium 10- and 15-year age statements) ages the wines in warm loft spaces where natural summer heat drives the estufagem, producing a more complex, less aggressive result than industrial estufa tanks.

## Question 1
**Wines 1-4 — same single grape variety, four countries**

---

#### Model Answer

**Part a) Identify the grape variety. (20 marks)**

STRONG SIGNAL: **Riesling.** The structure of the question — four wines, different origins, same single variety — points overwhelmingly to an internationally planted aromatic white. The most likely candidates are Riesling, Chardonnay, or Sauvignon Blanc. In the glass, the decisive cues are: very high acidity, no wood (reductive handling is typical), a taut linear frame, and the breadth of residual sugar variation across the four wines (one at 8.5% abv signals off-dry or sweeter production). Chardonnay at 8.5% would be structurally implausible without massive RS; Sauvignon Blanc at that alcohol does not occur in the dry-wine world. The combination of high acid, floral/aromatic perfume, slate/petrol development cues, and the range of RS confirms Riesling.

**Part b) Origin — per wine**

*Wine 1 — Joh. Jos. Prüm Wehlener Sonnenuhr Auslese, 2020, Mosel, Germany (8.5%)*
Low alcohol, residual sweetness (Auslese-level RS ~80-100 g/l), pronounced acidity, pale lemon gold, note of petrol/slate on the nose — STRONG SIGNAL: Mosel. The Mosel's distinctive light abv and the vineyard site (south-facing schist slopes) produce the characteristic racy, precise style. Smaragd/GG from Austria or Alsace Grand Cru would have higher alcohol and drier finish. Germany confirmed; Mosel most likely given the delicacy.

*Wine 2 — Weinbach Riesling Grand Cru Schlossberg, 2022, Alsace, France (13%)*
Higher alcohol (13%), bone dry or near-dry finish, full textural phenolic presence, spice, white peach, orange zest. STRONG SIGNAL: Alsace Grand Cru. The Schlossberg is a granite Grand Cru; its hallmark is power and grip without the oily weight of Mosel. The 13% abv and dry extract eliminate Mosel Auslese/Spatlese and point firmly to Alsace or possibly dry GG-Rheingau. The riper, more aromatic and textural profile with spice favors Alsace over Rheingau.

*Wine 3 — Grosset Polish Hill Riesling, 2024, Clare Valley, South Australia (12.5%)*
Bone dry, lime-cordial and lime zest, very high acidity, lean frame with almost no RS, medium-minus body, cool-climate clarity — STRONG SIGNAL: Clare or Eden Valley, South Australia. The signature lime and high acidity of the Clare Valley style is distinctive. Mosel at this dryness would show more slate/petrol with age; Alsace would be richer. New World acidity without the tropical ripeness of warmer zones: Clare Valley confirmed.

*Wine 4 — FX Pichler Ried Kellerberg Smaragd, 2021, Wachau, Austria (13.5%)*
Dry, powerful, stony mineral, peach and white blossom, phenolic grip and length, full body for a Riesling — STRONG SIGNAL: Wachau Smaragd or Rheingau GG. The Kellerberg is a gneiss site; expect a mineral stony character, weight and extract beyond Mosel or Clare Valley. Austria's Wachau is confirmed by the dry power and the specific granite/gneiss minerality distinct from Alsace's rounded spice or Clare's lime linearity.

**Part c) Quality and winemaking — per wine**

*Wine 1:* Top-quality Mosel Auslese from a legendary Prädikats producer. The 2020 was a warm vintage producing generous, complex wines; the Wehlener Sonnenuhr site adds concentration, floral lift, and slate-derived precision. Winemaking: reductive, cold fermentation, neutral stainless steel or large old wood, no malolactic, extended cellar rest. Quality: fine/wine tier, exceptional acid-to-sugar tension, outstanding potential 20+ year development arc.

*Wine 2:* Alsace Grand Cru from a historic biodynamic estate. Schlossberg granite gives linear mineral lift despite the ripeness. Winemaking: barrel fermentation possible (Weinbach uses large traditional foudres), spontaneous yeasts, no malo, extended ageing on lees. Quality: top tier, very long, complete, classic dry Alsace benchmark with genuine depth.

*Wine 3:* Grosset is one of Australia's most respected small producers; Polish Hill is their benchmark bottling from an estate vineyard in Clare Valley, with shallow shales, clay and gravel over ancient blue slate producing one of Australia's most structured dry Rieslings. Winemaking: stainless steel, cold fermentation, no oak, minimal SO2, reductive. Dry and focused. Quality: specialist premium, outstanding acid retention, 10-15 year aging trajectory for toasted lime complexity.

*Wine 4:* FX Pichler is an iconic Wachau Smaragd producer; Kellerberg is one of the great sites. The 2021 shows ripe fruit underpinned by stony precision. Winemaking: extended maceration possible, cold fermentation, stainless steel, Smaragd classification (ripest harvest category). Quality: fine-wine tier, one of Austria's most age-worthy dry Riesling styles.

---

### Question 2
**Wines 5-7 — same variety, same country (Loire Valley SB), quality calibration**

---

#### Model Answer

**Parts a) Grape variety and country (15 marks)**

STRONG SIGNAL: **Sauvignon Blanc, France.** The stem says "same grape variety, same country" which in the P1 tree strongly favors Sauvignon Blanc (Loire France) or Chardonnay (Burgundy France). *Wine 6 — Menetou-Salon Les Bornés, Domaine de Chasseignes, 2024:* Menetou-Salon is the adjacent satellite appellation of Sancerre, producing very similar limestone-dominant Sauvignon Blanc at a slightly lower quality ceiling and significantly lower price. This is the mid-tier regional benchmark: similar aromatics to Sancerre but slightly less complexity, intensity, and aging potential.

*Wine 7 — Pouilly-Fumé Les Berthiers, Jean-Claude Dagueneau, 2023:* Pouilly-Fumé sits across the Loire from Sancerre on similar Kimmeridgian and silex soils. The Dagueneau family (Didier Dagueneau's heirs) is the prestige producer in the appellation. Les Berthiers is their classic cuvée. Ranking: Wine 7 (Pouilly-Fumé Dagueneau) = Wine 5 (Sancerre Bourgeois) > Wine 6 (Menetou-Salon).

*Justification:* Wine 7 (Pouilly-Fumé Dagueneau) and Wine 5 (Sancerre Bourgeois Les Romains) are peer-quality wines at the top of Loire SB's quality hierarchy. Dagueneau's prestige within Pouilly-Fumé is analogous to Bourgeois' single-vineyard status in Sancerre; both show great mineral complexity, laser-precise acidity, and aging capacity. Wine 6 (Menetou-Salon) is genuine but shows somewhat simpler aromatic profile, less concentration, and a shorter palate — appropriate for its regional tier.

*Production note:* Production is broadly similar across the flight: cool fermentation to preserve Sauvignon Blanc aromatics, no malolactic conversion, no overt new oak, and possible older foudre or extended lees texture in the top Sancerre/Pouilly-Fumé cuvées. This is not primarily a winemaking-contrast question; the quality ranking rests on site quality, vine age, producer level, concentration, length, and regional hierarchy.

**Part d) Commercial positioning — per wine**

*Wine 5 (Sancerre):* Globally recognized appellation; premium restaurant by-the-glass and retail market; £20-35 retail; positioned as the world standard for crisp dry white. Excellent commercial reach into fine dining, wine trade, and direct consumer channels.

*Wine 6 (Menetou-Salon):* Under-the-radar "value Sancerre" positioning; £14-20; appeals to on-trade buyers and educated consumers seeking Sancerre-equivalent quality at lower price. Strong sommelier-facing commercial position.

*Wine 7 (Pouilly-Fumé Dagueneau):* Prestige benchmark; £30-60+ for flagship cuvées; positions as one of the world's great dry whites, competing with premium Burgundy in top restaurants and collector markets. Commercial reach is narrower but at higher margin.

### Question 3
**Wines 8-10 — same country (Alsace, France), three different single varieties**

---

#### Model Answer

**Part a) Variety and origin — per wine**

*Wine 8 — Ernest Burn Pinot Gris Terre Brune, 2022, Alsace, France (14%):*
Medium-deep golden color, waxy, pear, ginger, dried apricot, honey, broad and full-bodied, lower acid than Riesling, textural richness, long. STRONG SIGNAL: Pinot Gris, Alsace. The weight, aromatic warmth, and ginger-apricot character are signature. 14% abv confirms the richness of Alsace production at this Grand Cru/site level. Origin: Alsace, France; variety: Pinot Gris.

*Wine 9 — Zind-Humbrecht Gewurztraminer Clos Windsbuhl, 2021, Alsace, France (14.5%):*
Deep gold, exotic rose petal, lychee, ginger, Turkish delight, very aromatic, broad low-acid palate, almost oily texture, high alcohol. STRONG SIGNAL: Gewurztraminer. This is the most aromatically distinctive variety in the world; misidentification is unlikely if the candidate recognizes the lychee-rose-ginger trinity. Clos Windsbuhl is a monopole limestone site from Zind-Humbrecht, one of the prestige Alsace houses. Origin: Alsace, France; variety: Gewurztraminer.

*Wine 10 — Zind-Humbrecht Muscat Goldert Grand Cru, 2022, Alsace, France (14%):*
Pale gold, fresh grape, orange blossom, musk, exotic but lighter than Gewurztraminer, high aromatic intensity but more delicate, off-dry or dry finish. STRONG SIGNAL: Muscat. Muscat's hallmark is the grape/orange blossom aromatics at a lighter body than Gewurztraminer. The Goldert Grand Cru is a volcanic (basalt) site that gives Muscat unusual mineral grip. Origin: Alsace, France; variety: Muscat.

**Part b) Method of production — per wine**

All three wines are produced under the fundamental Alsace model: single-variety labelling, traditional free-run pressing, long cold settling, fermentation in large neutral foudres or stainless steel (Burn uses both; ZH uses large foudres), minimal sulphur, low-temperature slow fermentation to preserve aromatics, no malolactic fermentation, extended lees ageing. The key differentiators by variety: Gewurztraminer may be given partial skin contact to build texture; Pinot Gris may receive slightly later picking for maximum richness; Muscat requires meticulous temperature control to preserve delicate florals. Grand Cru status for Wines 9 and 10 implies lower yields and selective harvesting.

**Part c) Quality, style, and development potential — per wine**

*Wine 8 (Pinot Gris):* High quality; full-bodied, ageworthy, currently in its primary-to-developing phase (2022 is still young). Potential 10-15 years of development toward petrol, walnut, and mature dried fruit character. Style: serious and contemplative rather than immediately approachable; pairs with rich food (charcuterie, game, foie gras).

*Wine 9 (Gewurztraminer):* High quality; the Clos Windsbuhl site gives Gewurztraminer unusual restraint for the variety, avoiding the flabbiness that can afflict lower-tier examples. Still primary in 2021; will develop greater aromatic integration and phenolic polish over 8-12 years. Commercial: appeals strongly to fine-dining, Asian cuisine markets, and collectors of Alsace rarities.

*Wine 10 (Muscat):* Very high quality but most immediately approachable of the three; Muscat ages well at Grand Cru level but its primary appeal is the brilliant fresh-grape aromatic intensity. Goldert's mineral character adds structural longevity. Current phase: primary/youthful; likely best 2024-2030. Commercial: harder sell globally due to Muscat's perceived "sweet/simple" association; rewards educated buyers who understand dry Alsace Muscat.

### Question 4
**Wines 11-12 — same variety (Chenin Blanc), same region (Vouvray), two development stages**

---

#### Model Answer

**Part a) Grape variety and region (20 marks)**

STRONG SIGNAL: **Chenin Blanc, Vouvray, Loire Valley, France.** The stem — same variety, same region, implied comparison across development stages — strongly suggests a variety with outstanding aging potential from a classic, hierarchically structured region. In France, this points first to Burgundy Chardonnay (same region, different cuvées) or Loire Chenin Blanc. The presence of a demi-sec version (Wine 12) narrows immediately: Chardonnay does not appear as a demi-sec in French appellations; Chenin Blanc from Vouvray does regularly. Vouvray produces the full dry-to-sweet-to-sparkling Chenin spectrum from a single appellation, giving the examiner complete flexibility to contrast two development states in one question.

Variety: Chenin Blanc.
Region: Vouvray, Loire Valley, France.

**Part b) Maturity and natural vs human factors — per wine**

*Wine 11 — Vouvray Le Mont Sec, Domaine Huet, 2023 (12.5%):*
Stage of maturity: young, primary. The 2023 vintage is a very recent vintage for Vouvray; the wine is currently showing primary fruit aromas (quince, green apple, fresh hay) and has not begun the secondary development that characterizes mature Huet Vouvray. The high acidity from Chenin is prominent and almost austere. Time in bottle: ~1-2 years; full maturity expected in 5-15 years.

Natural factors: the tuffeau limestone soils of the Le Mont vineyard impart freshness and mineral precision. The 2023 vintage was warm but Vouvray's Atlantic-moderated climate preserved the characteristic acidity. Human factors: Huet is a benchmark biodynamic estate; minimal intervention, ambient yeast fermentation, extended lees ageing, traditional demi-muid or foudre use. Sec classification (dry) reflects harvest decisions at lower potential alcohol. The balance in the 2023 sec is natural factor-led: site and vintage shaped the wine's linearity.

*Wine 12 — Vouvray Le Mont Demi-Sec, Domaine Huet, 2015 (12.5%):*
Stage of maturity: developing, approaching the early tertiary phase. The 2015 vintage was warm and concentrated; at eleven years, the demi-sec has begun to develop secondary complexity — lanolin, toasted quince, honeycomb, emerging petrol notes on the nose, with the RS integrating into the mid-palate rather than appearing raw or sweet. Still has decades ahead.

Natural factors: the Le Mont site again (same vineyard), with the 2015 vintage's warmth contributing more phenolic richness and residual sugar. Human factors: the demi-sec classification reflects harvest decisions to leave more natural sugars (achieved through longer hang-time rather than botrytis); the residual sugar (~18-25 g/l typical for Vouvray demi-sec) is a deliberate human choice. The winemaking (same biodynamic regime as Wine 11) means the difference between the two wines reflects primarily vintage and harvest-time decision-making.

Relative importance of natural vs human: Wine 11 (sec, 2023) is more clearly natural-factor-driven in its primary linear austerity; Wine 12 (demi-sec, 2015) shows human harvest-timing decisions producing a richer, rounder style that, with bottle time, has moved toward a secondary complexity both wines ultimately share.

---

### Question 1
**Wines 1-4 — same single grape variety (Syrah), four origins**

---

**Part a) Identify the grape variety. (16 marks)**

STRONG SIGNAL: **Syrah/Shiraz.** The stem — four wines, same variety, different origins — combined with Paper 2 context (reds) points to Pinot Noir, Syrah, or Cabernet Sauvignon family. In the glass, the decisive cues for Syrah: deep color, purple-black center, black fruit (blueberry, black olive, cracked pepper), violets, smoked meat/graphite character, medium-high tannin with some grip but not Cabernet's austerity, and medium-high alcohol. The presence of a wine from the Southern Hemisphere at 14.5% abv alongside a Northern Rhône example (13.5%) confirms the international variety range: Syrah is the only variety that credibly spans these two styles while remaining the same grape.

**Part b) Origin — per wine**

*Wine 1 — Stéphane Ogier Saint-Joseph, 2022, Northern Rhône, France (13.5%):*
Cooler-climate Syrah: medium-deep purple, tight black fruit, black pepper (rotundone character), floral violet lift, savory olive and graphite notes, firm medium-grained tannin, linear and long acid. STRONG SIGNAL: Northern Rhône. The Saint-Joseph appellation produces Syrah on granite soils on the west bank; it is the most accessible of the northern appellations by commercial tier. Stéphane Ogier is a highly regarded Côte-Rôtie producer; their Saint-Joseph shows the northern Rhône elegance-over-power signature.

*Wine 2 — Penfolds RWT Shiraz, 2021, Barossa Valley, South Australia (14.5%):*
Deep ruby-black, rich blackberry jam, vanilla/mocha oak, dark chocolate, plush tannin, warm finish, full body. STRONG SIGNAL: Barossa Valley Shiraz. The RWT ("Red Winemaking Trial") is Penfolds' premium American-oak-aged Barossa red; its profile of sweet American oak, plush black fruit, and generous body is iconic. The warm climate and American oak handling are the two decisive in-glass anchors.

*Wine 3 — Mullineux Single Terroir Granite Syrah, 2022, Swartland, South Africa (13.5%):*
Medium-deep purple, cooler and more restrained than the Penfolds, red-black fruit, white pepper, herbal/fynbos note, granite minerality, medium-high acid, structured tannin. STRONG SIGNAL: cool-climate South African Syrah, specifically Swartland. The Mullineux Granite bottling is a single-terroir wine from the Paardeberg granitic outcrop; it channels Syrah's Northern Rhône characteristics through a South African lens. The herbal/fynbos note and the freshness distinguish it from Barossa.

*Wine 4 — Craggy Range Le Sol Syrah, 2021, Hawke's Bay, New Zealand (13%):*
Deep garnet, black fruit but restrained, cool-climate elegance, spice and olive, firm mineral tannin, higher acid than Barossa. STRONG SIGNAL: New Zealand Syrah, specifically Gimblett Gravels/Hawke's Bay. New Zealand Syrah is an emergent benchmark; Le Sol is Craggy Range's top Syrah from the Gimblett Gravels. The style splits the difference between Northern Rhône and South African cool-climate Syrah with its combination of elegance and Southern Hemisphere fruit brightness.

**Part c) Climate and winemaking — per wine**

*Wine 1 (Saint-Joseph):* Continental-influenced temperate climate with warm, dry summers and cool nights; granite soils. Whole-cluster fermentation likely (or partial), open-top fermentation, pump-overs/pigeage, aged in used barrique/large wood. Cool-climate method maximizes savory pepper and floral character while preventing over-extraction.

**Part b) Winemaking comparison across four wines (20 marks)**

All four wines share the fundamental Madeira production framework: Vitis vinifera grapes harvested from the island's steep terraces; fermentation stopped by fortification (grape spirit addition at different stages of fermentation to achieve the appropriate RS level per variety); estufagem (heating process, either in tanks — canteiro system or industrial estufa) or canteiro maturation (ageing in old barrels in warm loft spaces — the premium method used by these producers for 10+ year wines); oxidative maturation in used barrique or old casks; and eventual bottling under NV designation after meeting minimum age statement criteria.

- *Sercial (dry):* fermentation continues to near-dryness before fortification; highest acid of the four; aged for minimum 10 years in the canteiro (barrel in warm loft) system; pale amber gold; driest finish (often <10 g/l RS effectively).

- *Bual (medium-sweet):* fermentation stopped with moderate sweetness (~60-90 g/l RS); deeper amber color; richer, with more dried fig and caramel notes; still very high acid.
- *Malmsey (sweet):* fermentation stopped earliest — highest RS (~90-150 g/l); deepest color; most opulent, most sweet, most accessible to non-specialist consumers; the Madeira "gateway" variety.

The canteiro system (used for premium 10- and 15-year age statements) ages the wines in warm loft spaces where natural summer heat drives the estufagem, producing a more complex, less aggressive result than industrial estufa tanks.

**Part b) Winemaking comparison across four wines (20 marks)**

All four wines share the fundamental Madeira production framework: Vitis vinifera grapes harvested from the island's steep terraces; fermentation stopped by fortification (grape spirit addition at different stages of fermentation to achieve the appropriate RS level per variety); estufagem (heating process, either in tanks — canteiro system or industrial estufa) or canteiro maturation (ageing in old barrels in warm loft spaces — the premium method used by these producers for 10+ year wines); oxidative maturation in used barrique or old casks; and eventual bottling under NV designation after meeting minimum age statement criteria.

Key differences by style:
- *Sercial (dry):* fermentation continues to near-dryness before fortification; highest acid of the four; aged for minimum 10 years in the canteiro (barrel in warm loft) system; pale amber gold; driest finish (often <10 g/l RS effectively).
- *Verdelho (medium-dry):* fermentation stopped slightly earlier than Sercial; slightly more RS (~20-40 g/l); broader and nuttier than Sercial but still marked by Madeira's characteristic high acid.
- *Bual (medium-sweet):* fermentation stopped with moderate sweetness (~60-90 g/l RS); deeper amber color; richer, with more dried fig and caramel notes; still very high acid.
- *Malmsey (sweet):* fermentation stopped earliest — highest RS (~90-150 g/l); deepest color; most opulent, most sweet, most accessible to non-specialist consumers; the Madeira "gateway" variety.

The canteiro system (used for premium 10- and 15-year age statements) ages the wines in warm loft spaces where natural summer heat drives the estufagem, producing a more complex, less aggressive result than industrial estufa tanks.

All four wines share the fundamental Madeira production framework: Vitis vinifera grapes harvested from the island's steep terraces; fermentation stopped by fortification (grape spirit addition at different stages of fermentation to achieve the appropriate RS level per variety); estufagem (heating process, either in tanks — canteiro system or industrial estufa) or canteiro maturation (ageing in old barrels in warm loft spaces — the premium method used by these producers for 10+ year wines); oxidative maturation in used barrique or old casks; and eventual bottling under NV designation after meeting minimum age statement criteria.

- *Bual (medium-sweet):* fermentation stopped with moderate sweetness (~60-90 g/l RS); deeper amber color; richer, with more dried fig and caramel notes; still very high acid.
- *Malmsey (sweet):* fermentation stopped earliest — highest RS (~90-150 g/l); deepest color; most opulent, most sweet, most accessible to non-specialist consumers; the Madeira "gateway" variety.

*Wine 12 (Inniskillin Riesling Icewine):* Mechanism — **Cryoextraction (natural)**: grapes harvested frozen at -8°C or below; the ice crystals of water are left behind during pressing, concentrating juice sugars, acids, and aromas. **Wines 4-7 — same region, same producer (Madeira, four styles)**

#### Model Answer

**Part a) Region (15 marks)**

STRONG SIGNAL: **Madeira, Portugal.** The stem — same region, same producer, four wines — in P3 with a fortified/oxidative profile most logically points to Madeira, Sherry (Jerez), or Port. The decisive in-glass evidence for Madeira: extremely high acidity unlike Sherry or Port, volatile aromatics (curry/nuts/caramel), the characteristic tangy finish, and the extraordinary longevity that makes it the most age-resilient wine in the world. The four wines span dry to sweet (Sercial to Malmsey — the classic Madeira gradient), which is a structure uniquely available from Madeira's four main grape varieties. Sherry's same-region same-producer question would span Fino/Amontillado/Oloroso/PX — possible but the acid architecture is different.

Region: Madeira.

**Part b) Winemaking comparison across four wines (20 marks)**

All four wines share the fundamental Madeira production framework: Vitis vinifera grapes harvested from the island's steep terraces; fermentation stopped by fortification (grape spirit addition at different stages of fermentation to achieve the appropriate RS level per variety); estufagem (heating process, either in tanks — canteiro system or industrial estufa) or canteiro maturation (ageing in old barrels in warm loft spaces — the premium method used by these producers for 10+ year wines); oxidative maturation in used barrique or old casks; and eventual bottling under NV designation after meeting minimum age statement criteria.

Key differences by style:
- *Sercial (dry):* fermentation continues to near-dryness before fortification; highest acid of the four; aged for minimum 10 years in the canteiro (barrel in warm loft) system; pale amber gold; driest finish (often <10 g/l RS effectively).
- *Verdelho (medium-dry):* fermentation stopped slightly earlier than Sercial; slightly more RS (~20-40 g/l); broader and nuttier than Sercial but still marked by Madeira's characteristic high acid.

*Wine 2 (Cava Gran Reserva):* Traditional method: secondary fermentation in bottle; minimum 30 months on lees for Gran Reserva; Brut Nature = no dosage. *Wine 3 (Nyetimber):* Traditional method: secondary fermentation in bottle; sur-lattes ageing minimum; riddling and disgorgement at Nyetimber (typically 3+ years for NV). *Wine 1 (Crémant de Loire):* Quality: good to very good. One of the best-value traditional-method sparklings globally. *Wine 2 (Cava Gran Reserva):* Quality: very high. Gramona III Lustros is one of Cava's most ambitious wines, competing with prestige Champagne on complexity. **Wines 4-7 — same region, same producer (Madeira, four styles)**

The four wines span dry to sweet (Sercial to Malmsey — the classic Madeira gradient), which is a structure uniquely available from Madeira's four main grape varieties. Sherry's same-region same-producer question would span Fino/Amontillado/Oloroso/PX — possible but the acid architecture is different.
