questions.text:
Wines 1–4 are all made from the same single grape variety. The wines come from four different countries.

With reference to all four wines:

a) Identify the grape variety. (12 marks)

For each wine:

b) Identify the origin as closely as possible. (4 × 7 marks)

c) Comment on the quality and capacity to age. (4 × 9 marks)

d) Comment on winemaking with specific reference to oak and lees handling. (4 × 5 marks)

---
questions.modelAnswer:
## Question 1 — Chardonnay Cross-Origin (Wines 1–4)

### Part a) Identify the grape variety (12 marks)

The grape variety across all four wines is **Chardonnay**.

The collective case: across the flight, a consistent structural signature of moderate to high acidity, medium to full body, no pyrazine, no petrol/kerosene marker, no lychee-rose aromatics. The fruit register spans green apple through ripe stone fruit and tropical characters depending on origin — a width of expression that is diagnostic of Chardonnay rather than the tighter registers of Riesling, Sauvignon Blanc, or Chenin Blanc. The susceptibility to winemaking intervention — oak, lees, MLF — is visible across the four wines in varying degrees. No other variety shows this combination of neutral base + winemaking canvas + latitude-driven aromatic range.

Distinguishing from alternatives: Viognier (excluded — shows apricot stone-fruit intensity and peach blossom with no chalk/mineral structure and would show broader phenolic weight across all four wines); Pinot Gris (excluded — waxy/copper tint and lower acidity profile is absent); Riesling (excluded — no lime-electric acid, no petrol, no razor-fine low-alcohol structure). Chardonnay is confirmed.

---

### Part b) Origin, wine by wine (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 1 — Meursault 1er Cru Les Genevrières, Domaine Michelot, 2021. Meursault, Côte de Beaune, Burgundy, France.**

Pale gold with good depth for a 4-year-old white Burgundy. Nose shows hazelnut, white peach, brioche, and a toasty struck-flint quality — the classic complex interplay of Meursault's rich fruit and winemaking influence. Palate is medium-full, with nutty lees-derived complexity, integrated oak (barrel-fermented with some new wood), and the signature Meursault roundness — broader and more opulent than a Puligny-Montrachet 1er Cru of similar age. The richness and weight, the hazelnut/brioche complexity, and the warmth of the 2021 vintage (a generous, ripe year in Côte de Beaune following the devastating frost) confirm Meursault. Les Genevrières is one of the three historically outstanding 1er Crus of Meursault (with Charmes and Perrières). Michelot is a classic, reliable domaine in the village.

Ruling out: Puligny-Montrachet 1er Cru would show more precision and linear acidity; Chassagne would lean more stony/nutty without the Meursault butter. The breadth and the opulence are diagnostic of Meursault.

**Wine 2 — Chardonnay 864, Oakridge, 2022. Beechworth, Victoria, Australia.**

Pale to medium gold; the nose shows white peach, nectarine, preserved lemon, and a delicate creamy/lees texture — subtle rather than overtly oaky, but with clear barrel influence. Palate is medium-full, fresh, with saline-mineral grip and a long, textured finish. Beechworth is a high-altitude (550–800m) cool-climate granitic zone in northeastern Victoria; the granite soils deliver a characteristic mineral tension and citrus freshness that sets Beechworth Chardonnay apart from the richer, warmer Margaret River style. Oakridge's 864 (named after site elevation in metres) is produced with high winemaking precision: wild-yeast barrel fermentation, extended lees, no heavy new oak — a deliberately Burgundy-inflected Australian Chardonnay. Ruling out Margaret River (more tropical fruit weight, broader structure), Mornington Peninsula (cooler, more linear), and Yarra Valley (lighter body).

**Wine 3 — Chardonnay Crystalline, Paul Cluver, 2023. Elgin, Western Cape, South Africa.**

Pale lemon-green, still very young. Nose: pure citrus blossom, granny smith apple, grapefruit, a taut mineral freshness with restrained oak — the hallmark of a cool-climate South African Chardonnay at early age. Palate is precise, energetic, with bright acidity and a lean, mineral frame rather than the fuller, more textural mid-palate of Wine 1 or Wine 2. Elgin sits at approximately 200–400m above sea level in the Cape Fold Mountains, cooled by maritime air from False Bay; it is South Africa's single most important high-quality Chardonnay sub-region. Paul Cluver is the defining estate of Elgin, farming sustainably; the Crystalline bottling is their premium single-vineyard expression. The wine's youth (2023) and the lean, citrus-mineral profile are consistent with Elgin's cool-climate tension. Ruling out Hemel-en-Aarde (slightly more stone fruit and cream), Walker Bay, and warmer Stellenbosch (less mineral, rounder).

**Wine 4 — Chardonnay, Hanzell Vineyards, 2021. Sonoma Valley, California, USA.**

Deep gold, more saturated in colour than the preceding three wines. Nose: generous butter, toasted hazelnut, ripe yellow peach, vanilla, a whisper of cinnamon from oak — the richest, most opulent expression in the flight. The palate is full-bodied, with broad texture suggesting complete MLF, significant lees contact, and a higher proportion of new oak. The alcohol at 14% is the highest in the flight, consistent with the warm Sonoma Valley floor. Hanzell is one of California's pioneering quality estates; founded in 1953, it was among the first US properties to use French barrique for Chardonnay fermentation. Their house style is deliberately Burgundy-influenced but richer due to the Californian climate. Ruling out Napa Valley (Hanzell is Sonoma); ruling out typical Central Coast (the weight and lees complexity here exceeds most Central Coast commercial expressions).

---

### Part c) Quality and capacity to age (4 × 9 marks)

**Wine 1 (Meursault 1er Cru Les Genevrières, Michelot, 2021):**

Outstanding quality at 1er Cru level — the wine clearly exceeds the Village Meursault tier in concentration, length, and complexity. Les Genevrières consistently challenges Perrières and Charmes as one of Meursault's finest sites; Michelot as a grower-bottler produces reliable, terroir-expressive wines across the range. The 2021 Côte de Beaune vintage was difficult (heavy frost reduced yields) but the surviving wines show fine concentration and structure. At £60–90 retail, this sits at the mid-point of quality 1er Cru Meursault. Current age: approximately 4–5 years. Drinkability now: yes, approaching its first drinking window, though still a little tightly wound. Will improve for a further 5–7 years; will hold well for 12–15 years from vintage. Positive trajectory: increasing secondary complexity (hazelnuts, mushroom, toast); negative: beyond 15–18 years, even fine 1er Cru Meursault from a generous vintage can become too oaky and flat.

**Wine 2 (Oakridge 864, Beechworth, 2022):**

Very high quality for its tier and provenance. Beechworth Chardonnay sits at the premium end of Australian white wine — Oakridge 864 competes in the same quality conversation as the finest Giaconda, Fighting Gully Road, and Sorrenberg expressions from the sub-region. At approximately AUD 80–100 (£42–54) this is a value proposition relative to comparable-quality Burgundy. Current age: approximately 3–4 years. Ready to drink now, but has a further 4–6 years' upside as the mineral core integrates. Will peak at 6–8 years from vintage; hold for 10–12 years. The granite-mineral structure provides a sound ageing framework; the controlled oak will not overwhelm as the wine develops.

**Wine 3 (Paul Cluver Crystalline, Elgin, 2023):**

High quality for its tier — this is among the top Chardonnays produced in South Africa, from one of the country's premier cool-climate sites. Elgin Chardonnay at this level competes with top Hemel-en-Aarde and the finest New World cool-climate expressions globally. At ZAR 350–500 (approximately £15–22) it represents exceptional value. Current age: approximately 2–3 years; the wine is still in primary phase and currently tight. Not yet fully showing its potential — the freshness and mineral precision suggest a wine that will benefit from another 3–4 years' development. Will improve for 4–6 years; will hold for 8–10 years from vintage. Positive trajectory: broadening texture, more stone-fruit development, fuller expression of terroir. Negative: beyond 10–12 years, even fine Elgin Chardonnay risks losing the citrus freshness that defines the style.

**Wine 4 (Hanzell, Sonoma Valley, 2021):**

Outstanding quality — Hanzell occupies an elite historical position within California wine culture and within the global fine wine context. Their Chardonnay is not produced in large quantities; it is consistently rated among the finest California whites. The 2021 vintage in Sonoma was warm and generous; the wine shows the concentration of a ripe year without the flabbiness of a hot year. At approximately USD 75–90 (£58–70) retail, this is priced at the premium California Chardonnay tier. Current age: approximately 4–5 years; Hanzell is known to need time and the wine is in a relatively closed secondary phase. Will benefit from 3–5 more years. Will peak at 8–12 years from vintage; will hold for 15–20 years. Positive trajectory: the butter/toasty registers will develop into a more complex, nutty-caramel-mineral character. Negative: the high oak and full MLF can make very old vintages feel heavy. Capacity to age is among the best in the flight.

---

### Part d) Winemaking with specific reference to oak and lees (4 × 5 marks)

**Wine 1 (Meursault 1er Cru, Michelot):**

Harvest timing: slightly later than average to achieve full Meursault ripeness (historically 13–14% natural potential). Fermentation: barrel-fermented in French oak (25–30% new oak typical at 1er Cru level at Michelot); natural/cultured yeast. Post-fermentation: complete MLF (the characteristic butter and roundness are strong evidence); extended lees ageing on bâtonnage for 12–18 months in barrel, adding the brioche and hazelnut texture visible on the palate. Maturation: barrel, then approximately 6 months in tank before bottling. The oak is perceptible but integrated — the medium body and the brioche/toast character confirm barrel and lees influence; the absence of aggressive vanilla/coconut suggests French oak (not American).

**Wine 2 (Oakridge 864, Beechworth):**

Deliberately Burgundy-aligned approach. Fermentation: whole-bunch-pressed, fermented in French oak barrique (moderate new oak percentage, likely 30–40% given the subtle creamy character but no aggressive toast); wild/ambient yeast — evidence is the slight phenolic complexity and textural grip unusual in conventionally-yeasted wines. Post-fermentation: partial or complete MLF (the creaminess suggests at least partial); extended lees contact for 10–12 months, bâtonnage likely to build mid-palate texture. No apparent fining or filtration. The restraint of the oak handling is the defining winemaking observation: the wine shows oak influence without oak dominance — the mineral granite-driven fruit leads.

**Wine 3 (Paul Cluver Crystalline, Elgin):**

The palate's precision and tension suggest minimal oak intervention. Likely fermented in French oak with a low proportion of new barrels (≤20%) or a combination of barrel and tank — the wine does not show the obvious struck-match or vanilla register of new oak. MLF: possibly partial, given the bright citrus acidity preserved on the palate (full MLF at Meursault levels would soften this); if MLF was not fully completed, the winemaking intent was to preserve freshness. Lees ageing: some lees contact for texture (the mid-palate has a gentle creaminess) but not as extended as Wines 1–2. The Crystalline style prioritises site expression over winemaking intervention — a nature-forward approach consistent with Elgin's identity as a minerally cool-climate site.

**Wine 4 (Hanzell, Sonoma Valley):**

Hanzell's winemaking tradition is the richest and most intervention-heavy in this flight. Fermentation: barrel-fermented in French oak with a substantial proportion of new barrels (typically 50–70% new, sourced from select coopers); natural yeast from the Hanzell winery culture (a historical feature of the estate's practice). Post-fermentation: complete MLF — the butter-and-vanilla mid-palate makes this unambiguous; extended lees ageing for 16–24 months, bâtonnage periodically. The full MLF + new barrel + extended lees combination produces the rich, opulent, textured wine visible in the glass. Oak is clearly identifiable (toasted vanilla, cream, slight cinnamon) but well-managed — the fruit concentration at this site and in this vintage supports the oak weight without being overwhelmed.

---

## Proposed annotation

F1 cross-origin Chardonnay question structured identically to 2024 P1 Q2 and 2022 P1 Q4 patterns. Four-country deployment (France/Australia/South Africa/USA) maximises the quality-calibration challenge — each origin has a meaningfully different winemaking philosophy and terroir signature. The question's sub-part structure (variety, origin, quality/age, winemaking) is the standard F1 format. Meursault in Wine 1 activates the classification-level quality expectation (1er Cru vs Village vs Grand Cru). Beechworth as Wine 2 (rather than the more predictable Margaret River or Yarra Valley) is a deliberate difficulty step — testing whether candidates know Victoria's diverse cool-climate sub-regions.

questions.modelAnswer:
## Question 2 — Mosel Riesling Quality Ladder (Wines 5–7)

### Part a) Grape variety and country of origin (15 marks)

The grape variety across all three wines is **Riesling**. The country is **Germany**.

The collective case: across the flight, a distinctive aromatic family of lime cordial, white peach, talc, and — in Wine 7 — the beginning of petrol development; acidity that is electric and high-tensioned, standing out against residual sugar in Wines 6 and 7; alcohol between 8% and 9%, confirming incomplete fermentation and deliberate RS retention as a stylistic choice; the combination of very low alcohol + very high acidity + residual sugar is uniquely consistent with German Riesling Prädikat wines. No other variety/origin combination delivers this profile: Alsace Riesling is typically dry and higher in alcohol (12–13%); Austrian Riesling GGs are bone dry at 12–13%; Clare Valley Riesling is dry and shows lime-citrus without the slate-mineral quality.

Germany confirmed by the three-wines arc from restrained Kabinett through richer Spätlese to concentrated Auslese — the Prädikat escalation is the defining structural logic of this question and is uniquely German in its formal legal architecture.

---

### Part b) Specific designation/appellation tier (3 × 7 marks)

**Wine 5 — Bernkasteler Doctor Riesling Kabinett, Wegeler, 2023. Mosel, Germany.**

Kabinett: the lightest Prädikat designation within the QmP ladder, requiring minimum must weights of 70–85 Oechsle depending on region (Mosel: 70 Oechsle minimum). Wine 5 shows low alcohol (8%), a delicate off-dry profile with moderate residual sugar (approximately 20–30 g/l), high but not rasping acidity, and a light, transparent body. The lightness is the key: Kabinett is Mosel Riesling at its most ethereally delicate — a style demanding finesse, not concentration. Bernkasteler Doctor is one of the Mosel's most celebrated single vineyards, a steep slate site in Bernkastel. Wegeler is a historic Mosel estate with Doctor holdings; their Kabinett from this site is a benchmark at its tier.

**Wine 6 — Piesporter Goldtröpfchen Riesling Spätlese, Reinhold Haart, 2023. Mosel, Germany.**

Spätlese: the second Prädikat tier; "late harvest," requiring minimum must weights of 76–95 Oechsle (Mosel: 76 Oechsle). Wine 6 shows slightly higher alcohol (8.5%), visibly richer residual sugar (approximately 50–70 g/l), fuller body than Wine 5, but the defining quality is greater concentration and length. Piesporter Goldtröpfchen is among the Mosel's greatest single-vineyard sites — a massive curved amphitheatre of blue Devonian slate above the Mosel bend at Piesport; the site reliably produces Spätlese and Auslese of exceptional quality. Reinhold Haart is the premier estate of Piesport, and their Goldtröpfchen Spätlese is a landmark German white wine — rich, crystalline, and precisely balanced. The step up in texture and length from Wine 5 is immediately apparent.

**Wine 7 — Ürziger Würzgarten Riesling Auslese, J.J. Christoffel Erben, 2022. Mosel, Germany.**

Auslese: third QmP Prädikat tier; "selected harvest," requiring minimum 83–105 Oechsle (Mosel: 83 Oechsle), typically involving some botrytis-affected berries individually selected at harvest. Wine 7 shows the highest residual sugar of the three (approximately 90–130 g/l), deepest colour (golden rather than pale lemon), the most concentrated and complex nose — peach compote, apricot, honey, a first whisper of petrol and botrytis complexity — and the longest, most viscous finish. Ürziger Würzgarten ("spice garden of Ürzig") is one of the Mosel's most distinctive sites: red volcanic porphyry and clay soils interrupt the usual blue slate geology, giving wines of unusual spice and exotic-fruit character. J.J. Christoffel Erben is a small-production estate producing one of the longest-lived Würzgarten Auslesen. Vintage note: 2022 was a warm, generous Mosel vintage; the Auslese shows the richness of a ripe year.

---

### Part c) Style, sweetness, and quality within designation context (3 × 12 marks)

**Wine 5 (Kabinett, Wegeler Bernkasteler Doctor, 2023):**

Style: delicate, transparent, dancing between dry and off-dry; no heaviness, no new oak, no oak at all — pure slate-mineral acidity and lime-blossom fragrance. Sweetness level: approximately 20–30 g/l RS — technically off-dry but at this acidity level, balance makes it register as near-dry on the palate. Quality: exceptional for its designation. Bernkasteler Doctor is one of the Mosel's most prestigious sites — Kabinett from this vineyard exceeds the quality of most Mosel Spätlesen from lesser sites. The vineyard's blue Devonian slate and steep south-facing aspect deliver a mineral precision that is the signature of the Doctor. Within the Kabinett designation context, this represents the tier at its finest: concentration and character that justify an asking price of £25–40. The wine demonstrates Mosel Kabinett's unique proposition — arguably the world's most sophisticated low-alcohol food wine, under 9% alcohol with genuine complexity and age-worthiness.

**Wine 6 (Spätlese, Reinhold Haart Piesporter Goldtröpfchen, 2023):**

Style: richer and more generously textured than Wine 5; the Goldtröpfchen site's particular character — a wine of unusual weight and length for the Mosel — adds depth to what Spätlese delivers as a category. Sweetness level: approximately 50–70 g/l RS, clearly off-dry on the palate, the sugar balanced by the site's crystalline acidity. Quality: outstanding — Reinhold Haart's Goldtröpfchen Spätlese is one of the Mosel's benchmarks at this level. Few Spätlesen from anywhere in Germany match its combination of length, complexity, and impeccable balance. Priced approximately £40–65 retail, it competes with premier-tier white Burgundy in price-per-bottle terms; in quality-per-price it arguably exceeds that comparison. The wine shows both the stylistic signature of the Spätlese tier (richness, sweetness, fullness) and the specific terroir of Goldtröpfchen (weight, length, purity) simultaneously.

**Wine 7 (Auslese, J.J. Christoffel Erben Ürziger Würzgarten, 2022):**

Style: the most concentrated, aromatic, and complex of the three; the botrytis influence adds layers of dried apricot and honeyed depth without making this a dessert wine in the conventional sense — the Mosel's naturally high acidity keeps an Auslese fresh and digestible despite high RS. Sweetness level: approximately 90–130 g/l RS; clearly sweet, though the acidity (structured and electric) prevents any sense of cloying. Quality: outstanding. J.J. Christoffel is a legendary small estate; their Würzgarten holdings produce Auslesen that age for decades. Priced at £60–100+ retail (for a relatively young 2022 vintage), this represents exceptional intrinsic quality. The Würzgarten site's volcanic red soil signature is perceptible in the wine's unusual spice and exotic character — distinguishable from Goldtröpfchen's more purely mineral-fruity profile. At this designation level, the wine's combination of complexity, concentration, and structural precision places it firmly in the outstanding tier of German Riesling.

---

### Part d) Quality ranking with reference to legal classification (18 marks)

Ranking in ascending quality order, with reference to the Prädikat classification system:

**Third (lowest):** Wine 5 — Kabinett. By the legal architecture of the QmP system, Kabinett represents the lightest tier of Prädikat wines and the minimum required natural sugar content. The quality of the individual wine (Bernkasteler Doctor) is exceptional within the tier, but the Kabinett designation establishes a structurally lighter, less concentrated style than either Spätlese or Auslese. A Kabinett, however great the site, does not aspire to the richness or complexity that the higher Prädikat designations achieve by harvesting later-ripened fruit.

**Second:** Wine 6 — Spätlese. The Spätlese designation requires 76–95 Oechsle minimum (vs. 70 for Kabinett) — the later harvest delivers greater concentration, more extract, more complex aromatics, and higher natural RS. Reinhold Haart's Goldtröpfchen Spätlese is one of the greatest wines at this tier anywhere in Germany, but by classification the Spätlese tier sits below Auslese in the formal hierarchy. The wine shows greater depth and length than Wine 5, confirming its superior position.

**First (highest):** Wine 7 — Auslese. The Auslese tier requires minimum 83–105 Oechsle; the selection of individually botrytis-affected and fully-ripened bunches at harvest produces the most concentrated, complex, and age-worthy category within the table wine segment of QmP (above Auslese sits the rare Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese, which are dessert wines in concentration). Christoffel's Würzgarten Auslese demonstrates the peak of what Mosel Riesling can achieve as an off-sweet wine: extraordinary aromatic complexity, impeccable balance, and the concentration to develop for 20–30 years.

The examiner should note that the IMW quality ranking here is a reflection of official German wine law's own hierarchy, which defines Auslese as superior to Spätlese as superior to Kabinett. The quality of each individual wine (all three are from excellent sites and estates) could in theory blur this ranking — a Bernkasteler Doctor Kabinett from a great year (e.g., 2021, 2017) can surpass a mediocre Auslese from a lesser site. However, within this flight — same region, same vintage year, three different designation tiers — the Prädikat ladder is the correct and legally supported ordering framework.

---

### Part e) Commercial positioning (10 marks)

**Wine 5 (Kabinett, Wegeler Bernkasteler Doctor):**

Positioned at the premium specialist end of restaurant lists and quality wine retailers in key export markets (UK, USA, Germany, Benelux, Japan). Priced at £25–40 in the UK and $35–55 in the USA, this occupies the quality-entry tier for Mosel Riesling and offers genuinely exceptional quality per price relative to Burgundy or Rhône at the same bracket. The primary commercial challenge for Mosel Kabinett generally — consumer confusion about sweetness (many assume all German Riesling is sweet) — is partially overcome by the Bernkasteler Doctor name recognition among connoisseurs. Trade-facing sales through specialist importers is the dominant channel; the on-trade in fine dining and wine-list-driven restaurants provides the primary exposure route.

**Wine 6 (Spätlese, Reinhold Haart Goldtröpfchen):**

Fine wine territory. Reinhold Haart is not a large producer; supply is tight. The wine is sold predominantly through specialist importers and fine wine merchants in the UK (Berry Bros & Rudd, Justerini & Brooks), USA (Skurnik, Terry Theise selection estates), Germany, and Japan. At £40–65, it competes for the same shelf and list position as village-level Meursault or Puligny-Montrachet — and frequently outperforms these in quality-per-price analysis. Commercial challenge: the Mosel fine wine category lacks the brand equity of Burgundy among consumers outside the specialist community. The growth story is in restaurants with sommelier-curated wine lists where Mosel Spätlese is increasingly positioned as a prestige, low-alcohol alternative to white Burgundy.

**Wine 7 (Auslese, J.J. Christoffel Erben Würzgarten):**

Cult collector and specialist market. Very small production; sold primarily through auction (Auction Nürnberg, Christie's, Sotheby's) and through specialist German Riesling importers. At £60–100+ even for a current vintage, the wine requires a consumer who understands German Prädikat wine and is willing to invest in long-ageing sweet wines. The primary export markets are Germany, Japan (off-dry Riesling has strong cultural traction), UK specialist, and the USA German Riesling enthusiast community. Commercial challenge: premium sweet wine globally faces market pressure from the trend toward dry wine consumption. The counterargument is that great Mosel Auslese is genuinely unlike anything else — a proposition that specialist merchants and sommeliers make effectively.

---

## Proposed annotation

F7 hierarchy question using a classic Mosel quality ladder — Kabinett/Spätlese/Auslese from three distinct estates but the same region. The stem ("ascending order of quality designation") is an explicit signal; the examiner is testing whether candidates know the Prädikat system's legal architecture and can connect it to quality observation. Using three different famous Mosel estates (Wegeler/Bernkasteler Doctor, Reinhold Haart/Goldtröpfchen, Christoffel/Würzgarten) rather than one producer adds origin-identification depth beyond a simple quality-tier exercise.

The low alcohol values (8–9%) and off-dry sweetness immediately exclude Burgundy and Alsace; only German Riesling delivers this combination. The Kabinett/Spätlese/Auslese trio is a textbook Mosel flight.
- Wine 5 (Kabinett): lightest, most delicate, off-dry, 8% → KABINETT confirmed.
- Wine 6 (Spätlese): richer, more off-dry, 8.5% → SPÄTLESE confirmed.

questions.text:
Wines 8–10 are from the same country and the same broad region but come from three different sub-regions. Each wine is made from a different single or predominant grape variety.

With reference to all three wines:

a) Identify the country and broad region. (10 marks)

For each wine:

b) Identify the sub-region and grape variety as closely as possible. (3 × 10 marks)

c) Comment on winemaking and style. (3 × 8 marks)

With reference to all three wines:

d) Discuss how variety and production method shape the quality and commercial appeal of each wine. (24 marks)

---
questions.modelAnswer:
## Question 3 — Northern Rhône Whites, Three Appellations (Wines 8–10)

### Part a) Country and broad region (10 marks)

The country is **France**. The broad region is the **Northern Rhône Valley**.

The case: all three wines share the structural signature of the Northern Rhône's white grape varieties — high alcohol (13–14%), phenolic/textural weight, and a stone-fruit to white-flower aromatic profile that is both intense and specific. The absence of the pyrazine signature of Sauvignon Blanc, the absence of Riesling's petrol-acid profile, and the absence of Chardonnay's lactic/oak-malleable neutrality all point away from other France regions. The Northern Rhône identity is confirmed by: Wine 8 (Viognier — apricot/floral/phenolic); Wine 9 (Marsanne — almond/wax/heavy texture); Wine 10 (Marsanne/Roussanne or Roussanne/Marsanne — stone fruit/herbal/fuller). The three-appellation structure within one valley, with three different dominant varieties, is unique to the Northern Rhône.

Ruling out Southern Rhône (Grenache Blanc/Clairette dominate; no Viognier-only appellation at this weight), Languedoc (lacks the formal appellation structure and the specific variety-site combination), Jura (different variety profile entirely).

---

### Part b) Appellation and grape variety (3 × 10 marks)

**Wine 8 — Condrieu Lieu-Dit Coteau de Chaillées, Château du Rozay (E. Guigal), 2023. Condrieu, Northern Rhône Valley, France. Variety: Viognier.**

Condrieu: the sole appellation in the world in which Viognier is grown as a premium variety producing iconic quality. The wine shows the hallmark Condrieu profile: intense apricot, fresh peach, white peach blossom, violet, a whisper of ginger, and a generous, almost honeyed mid-palate despite technical dryness; high alcohol (14%) balanced by phenolic grip rather than acidity; phenolic bitterness on the finish distinguishing this from a residual-sugar sweetness. Viognier is confirmed by: the absence of pyrazine, the absence of petrol, the absence of any lemon-citrus register, and the presence of the unique stone-fruit/floral/phenolic Viognier fingerprint. Condrieu is the appellation of origin (Viognier is grown nowhere else at this quality level in the Northern Rhône); the lieu-dit Coteau de Chaillées is one of Guigal's holdings within this AC, managed under the Château du Rozay label. 14% and the full, phenolic weight are consistent with a warm 2023 Northern Rhône vintage.

Ruling out: Château Grillet (Guigal-owned monopole, also 100% Viognier, but Wine 8 is a lieu-dit rather than an AC in itself — and Château Grillet shows slightly more restraint and longevity than the expressive young Rozay style). Viognier from Languedoc or Collines Rhodaniennes (IGP) would show less phenolic grip and lower quality concentration.

**Wine 9 — Crozes-Hermitage Blanc "Mule Blanche", Paul Jaboulet Aîné, 2022. Crozes-Hermitage, Northern Rhône Valley, France. Variety: Marsanne (dominant) with Roussanne.**

Crozes-Hermitage Blanc: the largest Northern Rhône white appellation, surrounding the famous Hermitage hill on three sides but producing wines generally less concentrated than Hermitage itself. Marsanne (dominant) produces a wine of heavy, almond-blossom/beeswax aromatic register, with a broad, almost oily texture and relatively low acidity; Roussanne adds floral complexity. Wine 9 shows this profile: almond blossom, white peach, beeswax, a slightly waxy/oily texture on the palate, and lower acidity than Wine 8 or Wine 10. The alcohol at 13% is consistent with a 2022 Crozes. "Mule Blanche" is Jaboulet's flagship Crozes-Hermitage Blanc — a well-known benchmark of the appellation.

Ruling out: Hermitage Blanc (would show greater concentration, length, and complexity — Jaboulet's own Hermitage Chevalier de Stérimberg is noticeably more powerful); Saint-Péray (Marsanne-only, slightly different weight and style, typically fuller).

**Wine 10 — Saint-Péray "Fleur de Crussol", Domaine Alain Voge, 2022. Saint-Péray, Northern Rhône Valley, France. Variety: Marsanne (dominant) with Roussanne.**

Saint-Péray: a small Northern Rhône appellation at the far southern end of the zone, producing still and sparkling whites from Marsanne (principally) and Roussanne. Still Saint-Péray is historically underrated; at its best it combines Marsanne's phenolic weight with greater elegance and floral freshness than Crozes-Hermitage, owing to the granitic/calcareous soils on the steep slopes above the town. Wine 10 shows: stone fruit (white peach/apricot), a distinct herbal-floral quality (more refined than Wine 9's almond/wax), good weight and length, slightly higher acid than Wine 9 — consistent with the diversity within Marsanne-based whites depending on site. Alain Voge is one of Saint-Péray's finest estates, producing both still and sparkling versions; "Fleur de Crussol" is sourced from the Crussol hillside above Cornas, a particularly well-exposed granite and limestone slope.

Ruling out: Condrieu (no Viognier aromatic signature — no apricot/peach blossom intensity); Crozes-Hermitage (Saint-Péray shows more refined floral character than typical Crozes).

---

### Part c) Winemaking and style (3 × 8 marks)

**Wine 8 (Condrieu, Rozay/Guigal, 2023):**

Vineyard: steep granite terraces of Condrieu, hand-harvested due to slope inclination. Fermentation: barrel-fermented in French oak (barriques, typically 20–30% new) or stainless steel depending on cuvée — the Rozay style under Guigal's direction tends toward partial barrel fermentation for mid-palate texture. The oak is present but not dominant; the primary character of the wine is Viognier's natural phenolic weight and aromatics, not oak-derived vanilla. Post-fermentation: limited or no MLF to preserve the Viognier's aromatic freshness (MLF in Viognier can strip aromatic intensity) — the freshness of the 2023 vintage supports this. Lees ageing: some, but typically for 8–12 months rather than Burgundy-style extended bâtonnage. Style: opulent, aromatic, textural — best drunk within 5 years of vintage; Condrieu is notoriously difficult to age (the aromatic intensity fades, leaving only the phenolic structure).

**Wine 9 (Crozes-Hermitage Blanc "Mule Blanche", Jaboulet, 2022):**

Vineyard: flat alluvial plains and gravel terraces around the Hermitage hill — the majority of Crozes-Hermitage vines are on less dramatic sites than Hermitage itself. Fermentation: tank-fermented with temperature control, or a proportion in barrel — the Mule Blanche style under current Jaboulet (now under the Frey family ownership since 2006) uses some barrel fermentation for complexity. MLF: likely partial to full — the waxy/broad mid-palate is consistent with MLF having occurred, softening the natural low acidity of Marsanne further. Lees ageing: 8–12 months, some bâtonnage. Style: broad, textural, almond-blossom dominant, not a wine for long ageing — best at 3–8 years. Commercial production is larger than most Northern Rhône appellations; this allows reliable supply for restaurant and on-trade placement.

**Wine 10 (Saint-Péray "Fleur de Crussol", Voge, 2022):**

Vineyard: steep granitic slopes above Cornas (Crussol hillside), hand-harvested. The granite base gives a more mineral, structured quality to the Marsanne than the alluvial Crozes sites. Fermentation: barrel-fermented in French oak (Voge uses a relatively high proportion of older barrels to add texture without oak flavour); partial or no new oak. MLF: may be partially avoided or avoided entirely to preserve freshness — the wine's relatively higher acidity compared to Wine 9 supports this. Lees ageing: 12–18 months, typical for premium Saint-Péray. Bottling: unfined and unfiltered for the Fleur de Crussol cuvée. Style: the most structured and ageworthy of the three wines — Saint-Péray at this quality level can develop for 10–15 years; the granite-derived tension supports slow evolution.

---

### Part d) Variety, production method, quality and commercial appeal (24 marks)

These three wines represent the Northern Rhône's white variety landscape: Viognier (Condrieu), Marsanne (dominant in both Crozes and Saint-Péray), and the Marsanne-Roussanne blend. The production approach differs across the three appellations in ways that profoundly shape both quality expression and commercial appeal.

**Condrieu (Wine 8) — Viognier:** Viognier is among the world's most aromatic white varieties and among the most site-specific — it performs as a premium variety only on the granite terraces of Condrieu and in a small handful of sites elsewhere globally. Its commercial proposition is based entirely on this uniqueness: no other wine smells exactly like a great Condrieu. The production challenge is the variety's difficulty in the vineyard (low yields, susceptibility to disease, narrow harvest window) and in the cellar (aromatic intensity fades quickly; timing of harvest is critical). Quality potential: exceptional when the site-variety-vintage combination aligns. The Guigal/Rozay expression is a reliable, commercially visible benchmark at £35–55 retail. Commercial market: specialist on-trade (sommeliers value it as a by-the-glass prestige white), UK and USA export markets, Japanese market (phenolic whites have cultural appeal). The primary challenge: consumer unfamiliarity with Condrieu outside specialist circles, and the short drinking window (3–5 years) limits the fine wine collector market.

**Crozes-Hermitage Blanc (Wine 9) — Marsanne-dominant:** Marsanne produces wine of unusual weight and texture; its low acidity and almond/beeswax character require careful winemaking management (oak, lees, MLF all play important roles in building complexity and preventing flat, flabby results). Crozes-Hermitage is the commercial-volume Northern Rhône white — the appellation's larger production enables consistent restaurant-list and retailer supply at accessible price points (£18–30). Quality: good to very good at best; the appellation lacks Hermitage's concentration and longevity but offers accessible, textural white wine at a compelling price-quality ratio. Commercial appeal: the Jaboulet brand (despite its post-2006 change of ownership) remains globally recognised and drives restaurant sales across UK, USA, continental Europe. The risk: Crozes-Hermitage Blanc is not a category that commands consumer loyalty or cellar-worthy excitement; it needs on-trade placement to find its audience.

**Saint-Péray (Wine 10) — Marsanne-dominant:** Saint-Péray's smaller appellation and steeper, more mineral sites produce still whites of greater structural interest than most Crozes-Hermitage. The variety-site interaction (Marsanne on granite) yields a wine capable of genuine ageing (10–15+ years for the best cuvées) — a proposition that Condrieu and most Crozes-Hermitage cannot match. Quality potential: high, but the category is underrecognised outside the Northern Rhône specialist community. Commercial challenge: Saint-Péray's name is most associated in popular wine culture with sparkling wine (historically the appellation produced mainly sparkling Saint-Péray mousseux); the still white category competes against this historical identity. The Voge "Fleur de Crussol" at £25–40 retail is a value proposition for quality Northern Rhône white — it rewards specialist merchants and restaurant sommeliers who champion unusual Rhône varieties. Growth opportunity: as consumers increasingly seek alternatives to Burgundy (cost and availability), structured Marsanne-based Northern Rhône whites offer a distinctive, intellectually engaging proposition.

Collectively, this flight demonstrates that the Northern Rhône white category encompasses three quite different commercial profiles: Condrieu (luxury, aromatic, brief window), Crozes-Hermitage Blanc (commercial volume, accessible pricing), and Saint-Péray still (specialist, structured, ageworthy). The production method — particularly the treatment of oak, MLF, and lees — shapes how each variety expresses its terroir and determines the commercial tier. The greatest wines of the zone (Château-Grillet, Hermitage Blanc from Chave or Jaboulet La Chapelle) show what the varieties can achieve at the ceiling; this flight sits at the conscientiously-made, quality-focused tier just below.

---

## Proposed annotation

F2 same-origin, three-appellation, three-variety flight covering the Northern Rhône's white appellation diversity. The stem ("same broad valley, three different appellations, each a different variety") is uniquely designed to test regional depth: the candidate must know that Condrieu = Viognier, Crozes-Hermitage Blanc = Marsanne-dominant, and Saint-Péray = Marsanne. Sub-part d (variety + production method + quality + commercial) is a 24-mark synthesis question requiring the candidate to tie all three together — the highest-value sub-part and the differentiating mark for pass-level candidates.

## Reasoning trace

Wines 11 and 12 are made from the same single grape variety and come from the same region of origin. Wine 11 is more recent than Wine 12.

For each wine:

a) Identify the grape variety and region of origin as closely as possible. (2 × 12 marks)

b) Comment on the current stage of maturity and potential for further development. (2 × 10 marks)

With reference to both wines:

c) Discuss the relative importance of natural versus human inputs in shaping the style and quality of this wine type. (16 marks)

---
questions.modelAnswer:
## Question 4 — Hunter Valley Semillon Maturity (Wines 11–12)

### Part a) Grape variety and origin (2 × 10 marks)

**Wine 11 — Semillon Vat 1, Tyrrell's, 2018. Hunter Valley, New South Wales, Australia.**

The grape variety is **Semillon**. The region of origin is the **Hunter Valley, New South Wales, Australia**.

Colour: pale lemon-green, still youthful despite being 7–8 years old — the hallmark of Hunter Valley Semillon is its very slow colour development even over decades. Nose: restrained and precise; lemon curd, freshly toasted bread, a first whisper of lanolin and honey alongside the primary citrus — suggesting a wine entering its first transitional phase. Palate: laser-sharp acidity (notably high, even for Semillon), very low alcohol (10.5%), bone dry, with a tightly wound, pure citrus and green-apple core. The structural signature — very low alcohol, very high acidity, bone dry — is uniquely diagnostic of Hunter Valley Semillon harvested early (typically at 10–11% natural alcohol). No other wine region regularly produces dry table wine at 10.5% alcohol from a non-sweet harvest; this alone narrows identification to Hunter Semillon with very high confidence.

Funnelling: Chenin Blanc Loire shares the high-acid/lean profile at young age but shows waxy/quince character and does not reach this extreme low-alcohol; German Riesling shares the low alcohol but shows lime-petrol and some RS; Muscadet shares the neutral profile but lacks the palate intensity. Hunter Semillon is the only match.

Tyrrell's Vat 1 is the region's most celebrated Semillon bottling — one of Australia's iconic wine labels, consistently rated among the country's greatest whites over decades of vintages.

**Wine 12 — Semillon Lovedale, McWilliam's Mount Pleasant, 2012. Hunter Valley, New South Wales, Australia.**

The grape variety is **Semillon**. The region of origin is the **Hunter Valley, New South Wales, Australia**.

Colour: deepening gold with bronze/amber hints — 13–14 years of bottle development is visible in the colour alone. Nose: the diagnostic Hunter Semillon development in full expression: toast, lemon curd evolved to marmalade, beeswax, lanolin, a distinctive toasty-smoky Maillard-reaction character that is unmistakably Hunter Semillon at 10+ years. Palate: still dry, acidity remains formidably fresh (Hunter Semillon's extraordinary acid preservation over time), mid-palate now showing generous honeyed depth, the finish long and complex. Very low alcohol (10%) — confirming early-harvest Semillon.

McWilliam's Mount Pleasant Lovedale is historically one of the Hunter's most celebrated Semillon bottlings (from the Lovedale vineyard in the Lower Hunter); the estate has a long track record with this wine.

---

### Part b) Current maturity and potential for further development (2 × 12 marks)

**Wine 11 (Tyrrell's Vat 1, 2018):**

Current age: approximately 7–8 years from vintage (2018). Current maturity stage: transitional — the wine is moving from primary (citrus, lemon, linear) to secondary (toast, honey, lanolin) expression. It is not yet at peak complexity; the primary citrus-intensity is beginning to give way to secondary development but the full Maillard/toasty/honeyed register of mature Hunter Semillon has not yet fully emerged. Ready to drink now: yes, with pleasure — but the wine is not yet showing its best. How long to improve: the combination of extreme acid, low alcohol, and bone-dry structure in Vat 1 from a strong vintage like 2018 suggests this wine will continue developing for a further 7–12 years (i.e., peak at approximately 2025–2033, with 2028–2030 being a likely optimum). When it will decline: great vintages of Vat 1 have been cellared for 30–40 years with outstanding results; a wine like this should hold well until 2040–2045 if stored correctly. The positive trajectory: deepening toast, honey, beeswax, and the famous kerosene-adjacent Hunter Semillon character that develops to extraordinary complexity. The negative trajectory: beyond 30 years, even the finest examples can lose freshness and become flat and waxy.

**Wine 12 (McWilliam's Mount Pleasant Lovedale, 2012):**

Current age: approximately 13–14 years from vintage (2012). Current maturity stage: in full secondary development, approaching its first peak drinking window. The toasty/honeyed/waxy character is richly developed; the palate has the generous depth of a wine that has been building complexity over more than a decade. Ready to drink now: emphatically yes — this is a wine at or near its peak accessibility for a moderately patient taster. The balance between fresh acidity and secondary complexity is at an excellent equilibrium. How long to improve: limited further improvement likely — perhaps 3–5 more years of incremental complexity gain before the acidity begins to lose its grip. However, with 10% alcohol and Hunter's signature acid, the holding potential is substantial. When it will decline: likely holds well for a further 8–12 years (i.e., the broader drinking window extends to approximately 2033–2037); at that point, the acidity will begin to drop and the honey/wax character will dominate without the freshening citrus backbone. The positive trajectory: a few more years will add even greater depth of toast and a beeswax-lanolin richness. The negative trajectory: the citrus freshness that currently balances the rich secondary character will eventually fade.

Comparing the two wines: Wine 12 is demonstrably more developed and closer to its optimal drinking window now, while Wine 11 still has its major developmental arc ahead of it. Both demonstrate the extraordinary longevity of the Hunter Valley Semillon style — a longevity achieved despite (or rather because of) the deliberately low alcohol and high natural acidity that distinguish these wines from any other region's dry whites.

---

### Part c) Natural versus human inputs in shaping style and quality (16 marks)

Hunter Valley Semillon represents one of the wine world's most compelling case studies in the co-dependence of natural and human inputs; neither factor alone explains the wine's existence as a style.

**Natural inputs — the determining framework:**

The Hunter Valley's climate is warm and humid by Australian standards, yet Semillon ripens early here — paradoxically, producers harvest at low Brix (approximately 10–11% potential alcohol) in late January and February, well before the late-summer rains and disease pressure that characterise the Hunter's difficult vintage conditions. This early harvest timing — which is a response to climate, not a purely chosen winemaking philosophy — preserves the extraordinary natural acidity that defines the style. The Hunter Valley's free-draining loam and clay soils (around the Broke Fordwich and Pokolbin sub-regions) retain enough moisture for the vine through the growing season but encourage deep root systems that add mineral complexity. The Lovedale vineyard (Wine 12) is planted on particularly well-drained alluvial soils that add a distinctive textural refinement. Critically, the chemistry of Hunter Valley Semillon under bottle-reduction — the Maillard reactions and phenolic development that produce the toasty/honeyed character over time — are entirely natural processes; no winemaking intervention creates these characters.

**Human inputs — the enabling layer:**

The style is also entirely a human invention. The decision to harvest at 10–11% natural alcohol is a choice — a producer who waited for phenological ripeness would produce a 13–14% wine without the distinctive tension. The decision to make the wine completely bone dry (no RS) is a choice that makes the high acidity bearable at young age and essential to the long-term structure. Both Tyrrell's Vat 1 and McWilliam's Lovedale are made with minimal winemaking intervention — no new oak, no MLF, no lees ageing, no barrel; fermentation in temperature-controlled stainless steel followed by early bottling. This radical non-intervention is itself a highly deliberate human choice that creates the conditions for the wine's natural development in bottle. Without the human decision to make wine this way — harvesting early, fermenting cleanly, adding nothing — the natural potential of the Hunter site would be masked by conventional winemaking.

**Relative importance:**

In the context of young Hunter Semillon (Wine 11), the human inputs (harvest timing, clean fermentation, early bottling, no oak) dominate what you taste — the wine's current character is largely a winemaking construct, because the natural development has not yet occurred. In the context of mature Hunter Semillon (Wine 12), the natural inputs (the Maillard reactions, the acid preservation, the site-driven mineral complexity) dominate what you experience — years of bottle development have overwritten the winemaking fingerprint. The genius of the style is that human and natural factors operate in sequence rather than simultaneously: human choices in the cellar set the conditions for natural transformations in the bottle to deliver the final, extraordinary wine. This makes Hunter Valley Semillon arguably the world's most perfect illustration of winemaker restraint as the prerequisite for nature's full expression.

---

## Proposed annotation

Q4 follows the 2025 P1 Q4 "natural vs human inputs" stem pattern, which appeared in the historical exam. The two-wine maturity axis (2018 vs 2012) from the same region tests whether candidates can distinguish the same variety at different points on the development curve — and write four-element maturity answers for both. The "natural vs human inputs" sub-part (part c) is the distinguishing intellectual question, worth 16 marks; the best answers will engage specifically with Hunter Semillon's unusual combination of human non-intervention enabling natural complexity.

## Reasoning trace

- Stem signals: "same variety, same region, Wine 11 more recent than Wine 12" → classic maturity-axis pair. The explicit maturity framing suggests F6 or a maturity-focused F1 variant.
- Universe for same-variety same-region maturity pair in white wines: Loire Chenin (Vouvray dry/demi-sec), Hunter Semillon, White Rioja (non-vintage/vintage contrast), Alsace Riesling (GC vs entry), Burgundy Chardonnay (1er Cru vs Village). The sub-part on "natural vs human inputs" is a strong signal for a classic-old-world or site-specific wine where terroir vs. winemaking is a genuinely contested question.
- Wine 11 (2018): pale lemon-green, 10.5%, laser acid, bone dry, transitional → Hunter Valley Semillon in secondary development beginning. The 10.5% alone eliminates almost everything else.
- Wine 12 (2012): deepening gold, 10%, bone dry, toast/honey/beeswax → mature Hunter Semillon at 12–13 years. Kerosene-adjacent development confirms.
- Confidence: STRONG SIGNAL for Hunter Valley Semillon on both wines. The low-alcohol/high-acid/bone-dry/no-oak combination is not replicated by any other major wine style.

## Study diagram assist

**Diagram used:** `outputs/study_diagrams/p1_whites.md` — Section 3 (F2 Same Origin) and Section 5 (F4 Breadth, Semillon branch) and the F7 Hierarchy maturity node.

**Routing step by step:**

1. **Stem routing:** Same variety? Yes. Same region? Yes. Maturity emphasis → F1 maturity axis variant (or F7 maturity).
2. **Variety identification (F4 Breadth):** Wine 11: Colour = pale lemon → AROMA? Not pyrazine, not petrol, not peach/perfume, not lychee/rose. "Wax/lanolin → Semillon or oaked Chenin" branch. Palate structural check: 10.5% alcohol, bone dry, very high acid → Hunter Semillon (the world's most acid/low-alcohol dry table wine). Not Chenin (which would show quince/wax character more prominently at this age and slightly higher alcohol).
3. **Wine 12 (F4 → OAK_OX branch):** Deeper gold, Aroma = wax/lanolin/beeswax/toast → "Wax/lanolin → Semillon or oaked Chenin" — the maturity markers (honey, toast) confirm this is developed Semillon, not young. Same variety, same region as Wine 11.
4. **Australia branch of F2 Same Origin tree:** Tree shows "Riesling Clare / Chardonnay Margaret R / Marsanne Victoria / Semillon Hunter" — Semillon Hunter is explicitly in the tree. Both wines route cleanly to this node.
5. **Maturity assessment (F7 node applied to F1 context):** Wine 11: Moderate depth of development → transitional, not yet peak. Wine 12: Concentrated, long, fully developed → approaching peak/in peak window. Conservative rule: do not underestimate the development of Wine 12 or overestimate the development of Wine 11.
6. **Natural vs human inputs:** Not a tree node, but the F5 Method tree is instructive — Hunter Semillon sits on the "Nature-dominant: pure mineral, low alc, no oak" branch, explicitly showing that the Mosel Riesling and Hunter Semillon both fall into this category.
7. **Where the tree might mislead:** Wine 11 (young, pale, citrus-lean) could initially route through "Citrus/apple/chalk/restraint → CHARD → Steel, chalk → CHABLIS" before the extreme low alcohol and bone-dry acidity redirect to Hunter Semillon. The sub-10.5% alcohol reading is the decisive correction.
8. **Recovery if wrong:** If Wine 12 is misidentified as aged white Burgundy (honey/toast/wax are shared markers), the palate structure corrects: Burgundy Chardonnay at 12–14 years shows MLF-softened texture and oak integration, not the electric-fresh acidity and bone-dry structure of Hunter Semillon. Revise to Semillon.

With reference to all four wines:

a) Identify the grape variety. (16 marks)

For each wine:

b) Identify the origin as closely as possible. (4 × 8 marks)

c) Comment on how climate, oak handling, and winemaking have shaped the style and quality of the wine. (4 × 11 marks)

questions.modelAnswer:
## Question 1 — Wines 1–4: Grenache/Garnacha cross-origin

*Wines 1–4 are all made predominantly from the same single grape variety. The wines come from four different countries.*

---

### a) Identify the grape variety. (16 marks)

**Grenache / Garnacha**

The structural fingerprint common to all four wines points decisively to Grenache. The shared profile is: elevated alcohol (13.5–14.5%), moderate-to-low acidity, soft to moderate fine-grained tannin, and a fruit expression ranging from kirsch and dried strawberry through to garrigue and meat. Grenache is characteristically low in natural acidity and tannin yet accumulates sugar rapidly, producing wines of density and warmth without the structural weight of Syrah or the tannic grip of Cabernet Sauvignon. The wines span France, Spain, Australia, and Italy, consistent with the global reach of this variety under its regional synonyms (Garnacha in Spain, Cannonau in Sardinia). Alternative varieties with warm-climate weight at 14–14.5% — Mourvèdre, Monastrell, Zinfandel — were considered and ruled out: Mourvèdre shows darker fruit and more savage tannin; Zinfandel brings higher volatile acidity and jammy fruit at this alcohol; Monastrell is denser and more extracted. The consistency of soft tannin, warm kirsch fruit, and structural warmth across the flight confirms Grenache.

---

### b) Identify the origin as closely as possible. (4 × 8 marks)

**Wine 1 — Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Southern Rhône Valley, France**

The deepest complexity and most layered garrigue, lavender, and kirsch character in the flight, with the highest alcohol (14.5%) and a structured mid-palate suggesting multi-variety blending. The density, polished tannin, and length point to Châteauneuf-du-Pape rather than a lesser Southern Rhône appellation. Gigondas was considered but typically shows more rustic tannin and less aromatic refinement. The specific producer profile (Clos des Papes consistently blends 20+ varieties including significant Mourvèdre) explains the added structure relative to a Grenache-dominant CdP.

**Wine 2 — Campo de Borja, Aragón, Spain**

The distinctly concentrated black-fruit and violet character, with plush body, ripe chocolatey tannin, and evident oak integration, locates this in the Spanish Garnacha renaissance — most plausibly Campo de Borja or Cariñena. The specific elevation of high-altitude old vines in Campo de Borja (Alto Moncayo, 900m+) produces a density and aromatic lift that distinguishes it from flatter, jammy Garnacha. Priorat was ruled out: Priorat typically shows more mineral austerity and higher extraction from llicorella slate soils. Calatayud shows a similar profile but at lower concentration. The sweet oak and fruit-forward intensity point to modern international-style Campo de Borja.

**Wine 3 — McLaren Vale, South Australia**

The warmest, most glyceric, and most generously fruited wine in the flight, with dark plum, mocha, dark chocolate, and sweet oak, yet with characteristic McLaren Vale savouriness and iron-like minerality on the finish. Alcohol at 14% and the soft, almost silky tannin are hallmarks of Grenache from this sub-appellation. Barossa Grenache was considered (typically broader, more jammy) but the savoury mineral note tilts this toward McLaren Vale. Clare Valley produces Grenache at lower alcohol; Coonawarra is Cabernet country. The old-vine register and estate focus (Yangarra's bushnine old vines) produce a wine between New and Old World in its glycerol richness.

**Wine 4 — Cannonau di Sardegna, Sardinia, Italy**

The lightest in the flight at 13.5%, with dried cherry, sun-dried tomato, dried herbs, leather, and slightly elevated tannin suggesting the Sardinian expression of Grenache (Cannonau). The DOC Riserva tier from Sella & Mosca indicates minimum 12 months oak ageing. Italy's Sardinia makes Grenache in a distinctly Mediterranean-rustic register — less plush than Spain, less glyceric than Australia, less herb-laden than the Southern Rhône. Cannonau di Sardegna DOC spans the island; the Riserva designation requires higher minimum alcohol and extended ageing, consistent with the drier, more structured profile observed.

---

### c) Comment on how climate, oak handling, and winemaking have shaped the style and quality of the wine. (4 × 11 marks)

**Wine 1 — Clos des Papes, Châteauneuf-du-Pape 2021**

The warm, dry Mediterranean climate of the Southern Rhône yields ripe Grenache reliably, but 2021 was a more classic, cooler vintage with good acidity retention, evident in the fresher aromatic lift compared to the heavy vintages of 2019 or 2020. Clos des Papes' winemaking philosophy is classically Rhône-restrained: no new oak, with maturation in large foudres preserving fruit purity while allowing controlled micro-oxygenation. The result is integration and polish without new-oak sweetness. Multi-variety blending (approximately 70% Grenache with Mourvèdre, Syrah, and others) adds structural complexity beyond what pure Grenache could achieve. Quality is at the top of the CdP appellation — among the leading 10–12 estates historically — with the 2021 vintage presenting as one of the finest in recent memory for its balance of freshness and depth. Very high quality, at or near Grand Vin status within the appellation.

**Wine 2 — Bodegas Alto Moncayo, Campo de Borja 2021**

The extreme continental climate of Campo de Borja (Aragón interior) — cold winters, hot summers, high diurnal range at altitude — produces concentrated Garnacha with preserved acidity. The 900m altitude of the Alto Moncayo estate moderates ripening and produces violet-tinged aromatics atypical of lower-altitude Garnacha. Winemaking is modern-international: evidently new French oak, full extraction, and a long maceration. The result is a wine of international rather than traditional Spanish character — high density, sweetened by new oak, with fruit purity and structure. This is premium single-estate Garnacha aimed at the international fine-wine market rather than the volume tier. Quality is high for the DO — a flagship wine from one of Aragón's most ambitious modern producers — but the oak influence at this stage overshadows terroir expression slightly. Should integrate well with 3–5 further years.

**Wine 3 — Yangarra Estate, McLaren Vale 2021**

McLaren Vale's warm Mediterranean climate, combined with the cooling influence of the Gulf St Vincent, produces Grenache of exceptional ripeness and glycerol richness. Yangarra's old bush-vine Grenache (planted 1946) produces limited yields, concentrated must, and a wine of very high quality by any benchmark. Winemaking is natural-influence — minimal intervention, wild yeasts, no new oak (old puncheons or concrete), and unfined/unfiltered — which preserves the savoury iron-like mineral character alongside the soft dark fruit. The lack of new oak is significant: what appears to be density comes from fruit concentration rather than barrel, giving the wine authenticity and individuality. The 14% alcohol is well-integrated, not hot. This is among the top tier of Australian Grenache production, with quality comparable to a Premier Cru level in weight and seriousness.

**Wine 4 — Sella & Mosca, Cannonau di Sardegna Riserva 2020**

Sardinia's hot, dry, windy climate (Tramontane and Mistral analogues) produces Cannonau of firm structure and desiccated fruit character. The 2020 vintage was warm and relatively even across the island. Sella & Mosca's Riserva indicates 12+ months oak ageing (mix of large barrels), which adds leather and spice without overwhelming the variety's intrinsic dried-cherry, herb, and earth character. The slightly higher tannin compared to the other three wines reflects both the Cannonau clone's structural potential and the maceration length typical of Riserva production. Winemaking is traditional Mediterranean: cultivated yeasts, moderate extraction, large-format wood. This is a reliable quality-commercial tier — very good within the DOC, honest and varietally expressive, but positioned below the complexity ceiling of Wine 1 and the ambition of Wine 2.

---

### d) Compare and contrast the commercial prospects for this variety in each country represented. (20 marks)

Grenache's commercial trajectory differs markedly across these four countries, reflecting contrasting levels of consumer awareness, production philosophy, and export infrastructure.

**France (Wine 1):** Châteauneuf-du-Pape is the commercially established benchmark for Grenache globally. Wines from leading estates (Clos des Papes, Château Rayas, Château Beaucastel) trade at £50–150+ retail and are listed in fine dining internationally. The appellation's name recognition functions as a quality guarantor. Export markets — UK, USA, Asia — are well-developed. The challenge is that Grenache is rarely mentioned on CdP labels, where the AOC name does the commercial work; Grenache as a variety plays second fiddle to appellation identity. Growth is constrained by small AOC size and vintage variation.

**Spain (Wine 2):** Old-vine Garnacha is Spain's most exciting commercial narrative of the past decade. Campo de Borja, Calatayud, Cariñena, and Priorat all play in this space, with Priorat commanding €80–200+ for its finest wines and the other DOs offering value alternatives at €15–50. The variety is now clearly labelled (Garnacha Viñas Viejas), which aids direct variety recognition, particularly in markets primed by the natural-wine and old-vine narrative. US, UK, and Nordic markets are the primary exports. The opportunity is in capitalizing on the value story relative to French equivalents; the challenge is differentiating sub-appellations in consumer minds.

**Australia (Wine 3):** Australian Grenache's commercial renaissance is newer but accelerating. McLaren Vale Grenache from producers like Yangarra, d'Arenberg, and Bekkers is finding serious on-trade listings and critic attention globally. Retail at £20–50 (£70+ for single-vineyard flagship cuvées), with growing interest in the UK, USA, and Scandinavian natural-wine markets. The variety's light-colour, soft-tannin profile has also created opportunities in by-the-glass lists. The key challenge is overcoming Australian wine's persistent value-rather-than-fine-wine commercial positioning in major markets; the opportunity is in the old-vine story and the sustainability/low-intervention narrative that resonates with younger on-trade buyers.

**Italy (Wine 4):** Cannonau di Sardegna has intermittent export visibility driven by two narratives: the longevity/health story (the Blue Zone association with Sardinian centenarian drinkers) and emerging fine-wine interest from natural producers. However, the DOC lacks globally recognized brand anchors beyond Sella & Mosca's volume tier. Export prices are modest (£12–25 for most Riserva). The opportunity lies in leveraging Sardinia's terroir uniqueness and the health narrative for differentiated positioning; the challenge is that the appellation spans the entire island without sub-regional identity, limiting premium pricing power. Specialist Italian off-trade and natural-wine channels are the realistic route to market.

---

---

## Question 2 — Wines 5–8: Two parallel quality ladders (Burgundy + Piedmont)

*Wines 5–8 are from two classic red-wine regions, presented as two pairs. Within each pair, the wines are presented in ascending order of appellation quality.*

---

### a) Identify the grape variety and the specific appellation as closely as possible. (4 × 9 marks)

**Wine 5 — Pinot Noir, Bourgogne AOC, Burgundy, France**

Pale, translucent ruby. Bright red cherry, raspberry, faint earth. Fine, silky tannin. Medium-low body. The lightest structural weight in the flight with the most immediate accessibility points to the entry-level Bourgogne AOC tier in Burgundy. The combination of variety purity, linear acidity, and lack of concentration confirms regional declassified wine from a serious Côte d'Or producer (Fourrier declassifies fruit to Bourgogne in lighter vintages). Not Village, not 1er Cru — the volume and concentration are too light.

**Wine 6 — Pinot Noir, Gevrey-Chambertin AOC (Village), Burgundy, France**

Deeper ruby than Wine 5, with more substance — dark cherry, earth, sous bois, firm but fine tannin, medium-plus body, notable length. The Gevrey-Chambertin Village appellation is evident from the added weight and concentration relative to Wine 5, combined with the earthy, slightly austere character distinctive of Gevrey soils (clay-heavy Comblanchien limestone). Not a 1er Cru: the concentration and length, while impressive, fall short of the layered complexity expected at Lavaux or Clos Saint-Jacques level. Rossignol-Trapet is a serious Village producer; this reads as a classic Gevrey Village from a moderate-to-good vintage.

**Wine 7 — Nebbiolo, Langhe DOC, Piedmont, Italy**

Pale garnet — the characteristic translucency of Nebbiolo. High acidity, drying tannin, rose petal, dried cherry, tar. The lighter body and youthful approachability relative to Wine 8 place this in the Langhe DOC — Massolino's declassified Nebbiolo, aged in large Slavonian oak rather than Barolo's extended barrel programme, with a correspondingly more immediate fruit expression. Barbaresco was considered but dismissed: Barbaresco is typically richer and rounder in its tannin at this stage; this has the leaner, more angular character of village-level Langhe from the Serralunga/Castiglione Falletto corridor.

**Wine 8 — Nebbiolo, Barolo DOCG (Vigna Parafada, MGA Parafada, Serralunga d'Alba), Piedmont, Italy**

More concentrated and closed than Wine 7, with greater tannic grip and structural depth. Rose, tar, dried herb, dark cherry, iron, and notable length. The Barolo DOCG designation and the Serralunga character (austere, mineral, high tannin from the Helvetian sandstone soils of Parafada) are evident. Massolino's Parafada MGA from Serralunga is made in a traditional style — extended maceration, large Slavonian oak — producing wines that require extended cellaring. This reads as a wine still in its tannic youthful phase (2019 is a superb vintage in Barolo, tightly wound in 2026).

---

### b) Comment on style and structural profile. (4 × 7 marks)

**Wine 5 — Bourgogne Pinot Noir, Fourrier**

Light body, fine silky tannin, bright red cherry and raspberry fruit, medium+ acidity, short-to-medium finish. Very accessible, charming, early-drinking style. There is genuine variety purity here — this does not read as thin or washed out, but as deliberately light, made for early drinking pleasure. The tannin is almost imperceptible; the wine is defined by its fruit freshness and linear acidity. Style: elegant, light-framed Burgundy at the regional tier.

**Wine 6 — Gevrey-Chambertin, Rossignol-Trapet**

Medium-plus body, firm but fine tannin, earthy-savoury aromatic complexity (sous bois, dark cherry, spice), medium-high acidity, medium-plus length. The structure here is notably more serious than Wine 5: the tannin provides a framework for 5–8 further years of development, and the earthy depth indicates genuine Gevrey terroir expression. The 2021 vintage in Burgundy was excellent — fresher and more aromatic than 2020, with good colour and structure. This reads as classic, serious Gevrey Village.

**Wine 7 — Langhe Nebbiolo, Massolino**

High acidity, medium-plus tannin (drying but approachable), medium body. Lighter in frame than Wine 8 with more accessible fruit (red cherry, dried rose). The Langhe DOC designation typically involves shorter maceration and less time in barrel than Barolo, producing an earlier-drinking wine that nonetheless conveys the variety's structural signature. 2022 was a warm year in Piedmont — the fruit here is ripe and the tannin less aggressive than a cooler vintage would produce.

**Wine 8 — Barolo Parafada, Massolino 2019**

The fullest structural profile in the flight: high-to-very high tannin (firm, grippy, persistent), high acidity, concentrated dark cherry, rose, tar, liquorice, and iron. Full body, very long finish. Serralunga's sandstone soils produce Barolo of particular austerity and longevity; Parafada specifically sits on a high-elevation south-facing slope that intensifies this character. The 2019 vintage is widely regarded as exceptional for structure and aging potential. This is a closed, young, serious wine — not approaching its drinking window in 2026.

---

### c) Rank the wines across both regions in order of quality hierarchy, justifying your ranking with reference to the applicable classification or designation. (20 marks)

The ranking must follow the legally defined quality hierarchy within each region, which defines the appellation structure, not subjective preference:

**Rank 1 (highest): Wine 8 — Barolo DOCG (MGA Parafada, Massolino 2019)**
Barolo is the highest DOCG designation in Piedmont's Nebbiolo hierarchy. The MGA (Menzione Geografica Aggiuntiva) Parafada is a single-vineyard designation within the Barolo DOCG, representing the top tier of the appellation — analogous to a Premier Cru within Barolo, though Italian law does not formally stratify individual vineyards above DOCG. Serralunga d'Alba is widely recognized as producing the longest-lived, most concentrated Baroli. Quality at this level commands €60–120+ retail.

**Rank 2: Wine 6 — Gevrey-Chambertin Village AOC (Rossignol-Trapet 2021)**
Within Burgundy's legally defined hierarchy, Gevrey-Chambertin Village AOC sits above Bourgogne AOC. It does not qualify as a Premier Cru (which requires a named climat designation) or Grand Cru, but it is a named commune-level appellation carrying higher quality expectations and production constraints than regional Bourgogne. The weight, length, and terroir complexity of this wine confirm the Village designation. Retail £35–65.

**Rank 3: Wine 7 — Langhe Nebbiolo DOC (Massolino 2022)**
Langhe DOC is a step below Barolo DOCG in the Piedmont hierarchy, legally permissible for Nebbiolo declassified from the Barolo zone or made from younger vines. It is an honest varietal wine of good-to-very good quality but legally and commercially subordinate to Barolo. Retail €18–30.

**Rank 4 (lowest): Wine 5 — Bourgogne AOC (Fourrier 2022)**
Bourgogne AOC is the widest, most generic Burgundy appellation and sits at the base of the legally defined hierarchy — below Village, Premier Cru, and Grand Cru. Even in the hands of a great Gevrey producer like Fourrier, whose Bourgogne includes declassified Côte d'Or fruit, the legal designation is the bottom rung. The light body and limited length are consistent with this positioning. Retail £25–40 (Fourrier commands a premium over generic Bourgogne peers due to brand).

**Cross-regional note:** Comparing Burgundy and Piedmont on a single ladder is not formally mandated by law, but the question asks for a ranking. Wine 8 (Barolo DOCG single-vineyard) is the most structurally complex and age-worthy; Wine 6 (Gevrey Village) is next. Wines 7 and 5 fall below these in their respective hierarchies, with the Langhe slightly ahead on structural seriousness.

---

### d) Discuss the commercial positioning of each wine. (12 marks)

**Wine 5 — Bourgogne Pinot Noir, Fourrier**
Entry-level Burgundy from a prestigious producer. Retail at £25–45, targeting the entry point of Burgundy-focused specialist off-trade and fine dining by-the-glass lists. Fourrier's name elevates this above generic Bourgogne in specialist merchant contexts (Berry Bros, Justerini & Brooks, Kermit Lynch in the US); consumers are buying the producer's philosophy at the most accessible price point. Domestic French bistro market and international Burgundy-focused restaurants. The wine is typically allocated — not supermarket-available.

**Wine 6 — Gevrey-Chambertin, Rossignol-Trapet**
Mid-range Burgundy Village at £45–75 retail. On-trade primary channel: fine dining and specialist wine bars globally. Export markets (UK, USA, Japan, Switzerland) are the primary volume drivers. The Gevrey-Chambertin Village appellation is one of the most competitive in Burgundy, with 25+ serious producers at this level, creating a crowded field at £40–80. Rossignol-Trapet's biodynamic credentials add differentiation in markets receptive to provenance and sustainability narratives. Japan and the USA (particularly New York, San Francisco) are the most commercially receptive export markets for Village Gevrey.

**Wine 7 — Langhe Nebbiolo, Massolino**
Entry-point Barolo-maker wine at €18–30 retail. Accessible introduction to Massolino's house style and the Serralunga character. On-trade and specialist off-trade in Italy and internationally. Functions as a gateway wine for consumers moving toward Barolo; competitive with other Langhe Nebbiolo from serious Serralunga producers (Cappellano, Rivetto). US importer distribution (Kermit Lynch handles Massolino in the US) drives strong export performance at this price point.

**Wine 8 — Barolo Parafada, Massolino 2019**
Fine-wine channel: specialist merchants, fine dining cellars, collector/investor interest. Retail €60–120+ per bottle, with the 2019 vintage commanding a premium given its critical reception. Primary export markets are USA, UK, Germany, Switzerland, and a rapidly growing Asian (particularly Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore) collector base. Barolo from a named MGA in a great vintage has cellar-worthy positioning that appeals to on-trade sommelier list-builders as a wine for futures and aged-list development. Not a by-the-glass proposition; primarily accessed at Michelin-starred restaurants and specialist fine-wine retailers.

---
